The mean absolute deviation, the average absolute difference between each of the observations and the mean value, is another intuitive measure of dispersion. Sometimes it is called the mean deviation or the average absolute deviation, and mathematically it is expressed as Mean absolute deviation  =  ∑ i=1 n |X i − _
X | _ n , (5) where  _

X  is the sample mean, n is the number of observations in the sample, and the expression |...| indicates the absolute value of what is contained within these bars. The mean absolute deviation uses all the observations in the dataset and averages out differences. It is considered a superior measure of dispersion to the range but is seldom used because it is difficult to manipulate mathematically and offers little insights into forming statistical distributions that can be used for modeling. Another measure of dispersion is the median absolute deviation, the median of the absolute deviations from the data’s median. It is expressed as Median absolute deviation  =  Median(|X i − Median(X)|), (6) where Median(X) is the median of the dataset, the expression |...| indicates the absolute value, and Median(|X i − Median(X)|), is the median of the absolute deviation. This is a robust estimator of dispersion. The next case study illustrates the use of the range, mean absolute deviation, and median absolute deviation.

Variance and Standard Deviation The two most widely used measures of dispersion are based on squared deviations from the population average, μ.
•  Variance, σ 2, is defined as the average of the squared deviations around the population average:

Statistical Characteristics of Asset Returns σ 2  =  ∑ i=1 n (X i − μ) 2 _ n . (7) The variance calculation squares the deviations around the mean, μ, to resolve the problem that the sum of negative and positive deviation is always zero. The variance of financial asset returns measures the variability of the asset returns, with a higher variance indicating greater risk. Variance is sensitive to outliers because squaring deviations magnifies the importance of outliers.
•  Standard deviation, σ, is the positive square root of the variance: σ  =  √

∑ i=1 n (X i − μ) 2 _ n  . (8) Variance is measured in squared units associated with the data, which may not be easy to interpret. To return the data to the original scale, taking the square root of the variance, the standard deviation, creates a more easily interpreted measure than the variance. Standard deviation is often used to describe volatility. In most cases, the dataset is a sample of the true population, and we estimate the population mean using the sample mean,  _

X , which is an unbiased estimate of the true mean, μ. An unbiased estimate is a statistical estimate whose expected value is equal to the value of the population parameter it aims to estimate, ensuring no systematic error in its calculation. We calculate the squared deviations around the sample mean, (X i −  _

X ) 2 _ n − 1  . (10) Dividing by the sample size, n, instead of n − 1, results in a biased estimator that will systematically underestimate the true variance. Bessel’s correction in the calculation, dividing sample variance by (n − 1), elim­ inates the bias when estimating the population variance but not for sample standard deviation. This correction compensates for the tendency of a smaller sample size to underestimate population variance. The correction n − 1 is also the number of degrees of freedom. “Degrees of freedom” refers to the amount of independent information available to estimate parameters of a distribution, with higher degrees indicating more flexibility in the data to estimate these parameters accurately. Here, the degrees of freedom are the number of observations minus one: for a dataset of 100 observations, there are 99 degrees of freedom. Note that, perhaps counterintuitively, the sample standard deviation, s, calculated as the square root of the variance,√ _

σ 2 , remains biased despite using Bessel’s correction! The proof is beyond the scope of this text, but this occurs because taking the square root function is non-linear. Consequently, the expectation is that the sample standard deviation will underestimate the true population standard deviation. Note that as the sample size and the number of degrees of freedom increase, typically when n  >  100, the impact of Bessel’s correction declines and the need to make the distinction between the increasingly moderately biased estimators and the unbiased estimators falls accordingly. Effectively, the bias is highly relevant when sample sizes are small and the dispersion of observations is high. Standard deviation is a measure of dispersion about the arithmetic mean, and we usually present the arithmetic mean and standard deviation together when summa­ rizing financial performance data because they depict both return and risk. When we are dealing with returns or data that represent a time series of changes, presenting the geometric mean, the compound rate of growth, is also very helpful because it depicts the long-term increase in value. Statistical estimates are directly influenced by the frequency at which the data are sampled or observed. When highly frequent data, such as daily exchange or interest rates, are collected at lower frequencies—for example, monthly or yearly—more time passes between each data point. This provides the price of an asset a greater oppor­ tunity to change significantly. Thus, the magnitude of returns calculated over these periods tends to be larger. This underscores the importance of matching the frequency of data collection with the purpose of the analysis over appropriate time periods to capture relevant trends effectively. In finance, the volatility of returns over different time periods is often estimated using the concept of scaling. According to statistical theory, the variance of returns over a longer period can be estimated by scaling the variance of returns over a shorter period. To estimate the variance of monthly returns, the daily variance is multiplied by the number of trading days in a month, approximately 22 days. When the variance of daily returns is σ Daily 2 , then the variance of monthly returns, σ Monthly 2  , can be approximated as σ Monthly 2    ≈  22 × σ Daily 2  = T × σ Daily 2 . The standard deviation scales with the square root of time. If you want to estimate the standard deviation of monthly returns from daily returns, you multiply the daily standard deviation by the square root of 22: √ _ 22 . When the standard deviation of daily returns is σ Daily, then the standard deviation of monthly returns, σ Monthly, can be approximated as σ Monthly  ≈  √ _ 22  × σ Daily  =  √ _ T × σ Daily 2    =  √ _

T  σ Daily. This scaling relationship is known as the root of time law: The variance of returns scales linearly with time, while the standard deviation scales with the square root of time. In practice, financial return series do not always follow the root of time law perfectly. The variance of longer-term returns often scales at a slower rate than pre­ dicted by theory due to the influence of market frictions, changes in the behavior of financial markets due to variations in economic cycles or market sentiment, sudden large and unexpected price changes, and fat tails, or leptokurtosis. All these factors can individually and jointly affect the financial prices and returns and influence the scaling properties. The next case study focuses on the dispersion of gold returns. We show that the observed variance and standard deviation in lower-frequency data can be higher than expected from scaling longer-horizon variance or standard deviation; this is a typical occurrence.

1.	 How do the effects of trimming means and winsorizing a dataset differ? A.	 Trimming means removes the extreme values, while winsorizing amplifies them. B.	 Both trimming means and winsorizing replace extreme values with median values. C.	 Trimming means removes extreme values, while winsorizing replaces them with specific percentile values. Solution The correct answer is C: Trimming removes extreme values, while win­ sorizing replaces them with specific percentile values. Trimming removes a certain percentage of the highest and lowest values from a dataset and then recalculates the mean with the remaining data. This effectively eliminates the impact of outliers. In contrast, winsorizing replaces the extreme values with the nearest values at specified percentiles (for example, the 5th and 95th percentiles), which reduces the influence of outliers while retaining all data points in the dataset. A is incorrect: Winsorizing does not amplify extreme values; it limits their influence by replacing them with less extreme values—specifically those at the nearest specified percentiles. B is incorrect: Neither method replaces extreme values with median values. Trimming removes the extreme values entirely, and winsorization replaces them with the nearest values at the specified percentiles, not necessarily the median. 2.	 What does the interquartile range in a quartile analysis represent? A.	 The range spread between the highest and lowest values in the dataset B.	 The spread of the middle 50% of the data around the median C.	 The average value of the middle 50% of all the data points in the dataset Solution The correct answer is B: the spread of the middle 50% of the data around the median. The interquartile range is the difference between the third quartile, Q3, and the first quartile, Q1, in a dataset and represents the dispersion of the middle 50% of the data points around the median, providing a measure of dispersion and variability within a dataset, excluding the extremes. A is incorrect: It describes the range, not the IQR. The range considers the full dataset, from the minimum to the maximum value. C is incorrect: The IQR represents not an average or mean of the data points but, rather, the range within which the middle 50% of the data lie.

Statistical Characteristics of Asset Returns 3.	 An analyst is examining the annual returns of a technology stock fund and notices several significant outliers. Which of the following approaches is most appropriate? A.	 Increase the weight of the outliers in the dataset to emphasize their impact on the fund’s performance. B.	 Apply winsorizing by setting the top and bottom 5% of returns to the values at the 5th and 95th percentiles, respectively. C.	 Exclude all negative returns from the dataset to focus only on the posi­ tive performance of the fund. Solution The correct response is B: Apply winsorizing by setting the top and bottom 5% of returns to the values at the 5th and 95th percentiles, respectively. Winsorizing may be the most appropriate method for dealing with outliers in a dataset without entirely excluding them. This method involves replacing the extreme values in the dataset with the nearest values at specified per­ centiles—in this case, the 5th and 95th percentiles. By doing so, the impact of outliers on the fund’s performance analysis is reduced, leading to a more representative and less skewed assessment. A is incorrect: Increasing the weight of outliers would distort the analysis by overstating their influence, which is generally undesirable when seeking a representative measure of central tendency or performance. C is incorrect: Excluding all negative returns would provide a skewed and overly optimistic picture of the fund’s performance. Both gains and losses are needed for an accurate performance evaluation. 4.	 The Bessel correction eliminates the bias in calculating which of the follow­ ing sample statistics: A.	 Mean B.	 Standard Deviation C.	 Variance Solution: The correct answer is C. The Bessel correction, dividing by n −1 instead of n, gives us an unbiased estimator of the sample variance. A is incorrect. The sample mean needs no adjustment as it is already an unbiased estimator. B is incorrect. Though the Bessel correction gives us an unbiased estimator of the variance, there will still be a bias in the sample standard deviation.

sections.title: Measures Of Shape Of A Distribution

blocks.x: describe, interpret, and evaluate measures of skewness and kurtosis This lesson focuses on measures of the shape of a statistical distribution. The moments of a statistical distribution, which includecentral location, disper­ sion, asymmetry, and the shape of the distribution, reveal detailed characteristics of a dataset and provide deeper insights into the data’s shape and behavior. Initially, we

Measures of Shape of a Distribution explored the first two moments—mean and variance—focusing on central tendency and spread. However, to fully understand a distribution’s statistical characteristics, we need to include the higher moments that focus on symmetry of the distribution and the shape of the distribution’s tails. Skewness Skewness is a measure of asymmetry of the distribution, where a value greater than zero indicates a distribution with a long right tail, or positive skew, and a value less than zero indicates a long left tail, or negative skew.
•  Negative skewness indicates that the left tail, or lower values or negative returns, are longer or fatter than the right tail and means there are more low-value or negative outliers.

•  Positive skewness indicates that the right tail, or higher values or positive returns, are longer or fatter than the left tail and means there are more high-value or positive outliers. A positively skewed return distribution of an investment suggests that there is a higher probability of achieving high returns compared to low returns. Exhibit 20 shows different examples of skewness. Kurtosis Kurtosis quantifies the combined weight of the tails of a distribution relative to the rest of the distribution.

•  A leptokurtic distribution, or fat-tailed distribution or long-tailed distri­ bution, has fatter tails than the normal distribution and contains more-fre­ quent, extremely large deviations from the mean than the normal distribu­ tion. A leptokurtic distribution has positive excess kurtosis.

•  A platykurtic distribution, or thin-tailed distribution or short-tailed distribution, has thinner tails than the normal distribution and contains less frequent, extremely large deviations from the mean than the normal distri­ bution. A platykurtic distribution has negative excess kurtosis.
•  A mesokurtic distribution has tails similar to that of the normal distribu­ tion. A mesokurtic distribution has zero excess kurtosis.

Statistical Characteristics of Asset Returns For financial asset returns, a greater likelihood of frequent, extremely large deviations—that is, thicker or fatter tails—is considered to be riskier. •  Covariance measures the joint variability of two random variables, indicat­ ing how they move in relation to each other. It is a bivariate extension of variance—that is, one that is dependent on two variables.
•  Correlation standardizes covariance and scales the relationship to lie between −1 and 1.

Statistical Characteristics of Asset Returns These diagrams show the tendency for the returns on an individual com­ pany to move along with the returns on the broader market. Quantifying the sensitivity of excess returns to market returns is a fundamental aspect of investment analysis and portfolio management. It helps in assessing both the expected return and risk associated with an investment. We will explore this relationship in more detail later. A high correlation means that the two variables tend to move in the same direction. Even if two variables are highly correlated, however, one does not necessarily cause the other in the sense that certain values of one variable bring about the occurrence of certain values of the other—hence the phrase correlation does not imply causation. Spurious correlation refers to a misleading appearance of a relationship between two variables when, in fact, there is none or it is not direct. This misleading correla­ tion can arise in various ways. It may occur purely by chance in a specific dataset or result from both variables being influenced by a third variable that they both have a relationship with, suggesting an indirect link. The next case study gives examples of various types of spurious correlation.

Spurious Correlations The monthly US retail sales of beer, wine, and liquor and the atmospheric carbon dioxide levels between 2000 and 2018 exhibit a correlation of 0.824, indicating that there is a positive relation between the two. However, there is no reason to suspect that the level of atmospheric carbon dioxide is as closely related to the retail sales of beer, wine, and liquor as this one statistic might suggest. As another simple example, consider the height of a newborn as she ages against the value of USD1 invested at the risk-free rate: Both will trend upward, leading to strong correlation, but it would be absurd to suggest there is any causality or common factor at play here or to expect the correlation to continue beyond a certain number of years! Two variables that are uncorrelated may be correlated if transformed by an operation—multiplication, division, addition, subtraction, and so on—with a third variable. In particular, this situation can occur when the third variable has significantly more variance. Consider the mass of a stone being slowly eroded by passing water and the value of CHF1 in US dollar terms: The correlation is probably insignificant over a reasonable observation period, but if we divided both series by, say, the value of JPY1 in US dollar terms, we would find a lot more correlation. Finally, as an example of an underlying relationship being at play, height may be positively correlated with the extent of a person’s vocabulary, but the under­ lying relationships are between age and height and between age and vocabulary. Investment professionals must be cautious in basing investment strategies on high correlations alone. Spurious correlations may suggest investment strategies that appear profitable but would not be so if implemented. Correlation is sensitive to the existence of outliers in a dataset and therefore may be an unreliable measure when outliers are present in one or both variables. When outliers are present, trimming and winsorizing can eliminate noise. Some degree of subjective judgment is often needed to determine whether outliers contain information about the two variables’ relationship.

X  is the sample mean. Because CV is a measure of relative dispersion, the amount of dispersion relative to a reference value or benchmark, it allows comparison across datasets with different means or different units of measurement. When analyzing financial returns, the coefficient of variation quantifies the level of risk (standard deviation) relative to the reward (mean return) and shows how much risk is taken for each unit of return. The inverse of the coefficient of variation can be interpreted as the unit price of risk, indicating how much return is generated per unit of risk taken. Furthermore, when the returns in question are excess returns or risk premiums, the inverse of the coefficient of variation allows for a meaningful comparison of the risk–return trade-offs associated among various financial assets and helps in evaluating which assets offer a more favorable balance between the additional returns earned over the risk-free rate and the additional risk incurred. An issue that may arise, especially when dealing with returns, is that if the excess return, r i − r f, is negative, the statistic is hard to interpret. Moreover, a low mean and a high dispersion, which can be observed in highly frequent data, such as weekly and daily returns, may limit the ability to interpret the coefficient of variation. This problem can be remedied by annualizing calculated weekly or daily returns and standard deviations.

blocks.x: •  Measures of central tendency, dispersion, skewness, and kurtosis describe the characteristics of financial data and help in making inferences about the distributional characteristics of data.
•  Measures of central tendency, including the mean, median, and mode, pro­ vide different ways to identify the central point(s) of financial data.

•  Measures of dispersion, including the range, mean median absolute devia­ tion, variance, and standard deviation, quantify the variability of outcomes around the mean, a central tendency, and how spread out the data points are from the mean.
•  Skewness indicates the degree of asymmetry in a distribution around the mean, particularly when compared to a normal distribution.
•  Kurtosis assesses the weight of a distribution’s tails relative to the central part of the distribution.
•  Covariance measures co-movement between two variables.
•  The correlation coefficient measures the degree of relationship between two variables, highlighting association rather than causation.
•  The coefficient of variation compares the standard deviation to the mean, allowing for comparison of data variability across different datasets.
•  Semi-deviation quantifies the deviations below a set benchmark.

sections.title: Introduction: Statistical Distributions For Financial Asset Prices And Returns

blocks.x: This learning module focuses on using probability density functions and distribution functions to estimate and model financial asset prices and returns. These approaches can be extended to economic information and similar investment decision-making processes. After an overview of fundamental probability concepts, we examine the charac­ teristics of some key statistical distributions and their uses in finance, investments, and financial modeling. We then examine conditional expectations—an essential tool for predicting outcomes based on scenarios—which serve as a foundation for asset valuation under uncertainty. We conclude by examining how conditional expectations and Bayes’ theorem contribute to forecasting and valuation. Subsequent learning modules will apply the quantitative tools introduced here in economics, finance, asset valuation, investments, and portfolio management. L E A R N I N G M O D U L E

Random Variables and Their Properties A random variable is a function that assigns a number to each outcome of an exper­ iment. In finance, random variables are often called stochastic variables, reflecting their inherent unpredictable nature. Random variables are categorized into two types:

•  A discrete random variable has a countable number of distinct outcomes. For example, a fair coin toss results in heads or tails, each with a probability of p = 0.50. Similarly, rolling a fair six-sided die yields outcomes of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6, each with a probability of p  =   1 _ .

•  A continuous random variable can take on an infinite number of possible values within a given range, such as picking a random number between 0 and 1 on the number line. When the number of observations is large, the distributions will converge to continuous distributions, as it does in the next example. Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 contrast the distribution of heads from 10 fair coin tosses, a discrete distribution, with the frequency distribution of daily stock returns, a “con­ tinuous distribution” because there are a relatively large number of observations, so it is well modeled by a continuous distribution. The coin toss graph shows jumps at integers, is zero between integers, and displays a prominent peak at five heads, indicating that the distribution of outcomes is discrete. In contrast, the daily stock index returns form a curve typical of infinitely many valued continuous variables. Accordingly, continuous variables are more useful in modeling such return series.

•  The unconditional mean, or unconditional expectation or expected value, is the probability-weighted average of the outcomes of a random variable over an infinite number of trials. For a discrete random variable where x i represents the possible values of X and P(x i) is their probability, the expected value is: μ X  =  E[X]  =  ∑ i  x i   × P(x i ), (5) where E[⋅] denotes the expectation operator that computes the expected value of a random variable from its PDF (for continuous distributions) or its PMF (for discrete distributions). •  The unconditional variance measures the square of the spread of a random variable around its mean: σ X 2   =  Var(X)  =  E[(X − E[X]) 2]  =  E[X 2] − (E[X]) 2. (7) The last expression in Equation 7, E[X 2] − (E[X]) 2, provides a quick way to calculate the variance, assuming the unconditional mean is pre-determined.
•  The unconditional standard deviation is the square root of the uncondi­ tional variance.

•  The unconditional covariance assesses the direction and strength of the linear relationship between two random variables, X and Y (though care must be taken in the interpretation as it is incorrect to think that a large covariance value is indicative of a strong relationship in and of itself): σ XY  =  COV(X, Y)  =  E[(X − E[X])(Y − E[Y])]  =  E[(XY) − (E[X]E[Y])]. Diversification across negatively correlated assets, such as stocks and bonds, helps reduce overall portfolio risk. In practice, investors may allocate a portion of their portfolio to stocks for growth potential, while holding bonds to stabilize returns, especially during periods of stock market volatility. This combination not only mitigates poten­ tial losses but also ensures that the portfolio remains resilient across different market conditions. Constructing a portfolio of assets with low, especially negatively, correlated assets reduces risk, leading to smoother returns. calculate, interpret, and evaluate the principal moments of key statistical distributions used in finance Understanding financial prices and returns often involves modeling the processes that an analyst believes drive the behavior of the financial markets and financial market participants. This type of analysis generally incorporates elements of randomness that are consistent with the structure of the markets, participants, and assets themselves. Probability distributions with specific distributional assumptions are therefore required to model the behavior of the random variables involved in modeling financial market prices and returns. These assumptions are critical in determining which model best predicts market outcomes for prices and returns, which in turn determines the success or failure of associated investment strategies. In this lesson, we look at several distributions and characterize the type of situations in which each distribution is likely to be most appropriate to use. Our focus is on the uniform, binomial, Poisson, normal, log-normal, and logistic distributions. Discrete Statistical Distributions Discrete Uniform Distribution: Finite number of equally likely outcomes The uniform distribution is a type of probability distribution where each of the out­ comes within a specified range is equally likely. It can be either discrete or continuous. First, we cover the discrete uniform distribution with the following section covering the continuous uniform distribution. The discrete uniform distribution consists of a finite number of equally spaced outcomes, each with equal probability. For example, the outcomes from the roll of a fair six-sided die create the uniform distribution for whole integers between 1 and 6. (10) Binomial Distribution: Modeling binary outcomes The binomial distribution models the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials, where each trial has two possible outcomes: success or failure. The probability of success is p, and the probability of failure is q = 1 − p. It builds on the Bernoulli distribution, a discrete distribution with one trial and two possible outcomes, where success occurs with probability p and failure occurs with probability 1 − p. The binomial distribution is widely used in modeling events with binary outcomes, such as the success or failure of an investment or the up or down movement of stock prices over a fixed number of periods. One very prevalent application is the binomial option pricing model, where the binomial distribution models the price of options by simulating different paths for an asset’s price and their associated probabilities. Earlier modules used the binomial asset pricing model for one-period valuation of options and projects. The binomial model to price assets assumes that the asset price changes in simple, discrete, step-by-step increments over specific time periods. The model assumes that in each time period, the asset price can only move up or down to certain levels from its current level. At each step, there are two possible outcomes: The price goes up or down. The model considers all the potential price paths and their associated probabilities from which a value can be derived. Essentially, continuous changes in asset prices are broken down into a series of small, incremental, discrete steps.

Poisson Distribution: Modeling discrete rare events The Poisson distribution is applied to model the number of events occurring within a fixed interval of time or space, assuming the events happen independently at a known constant rate of λ per unit of time. It can be shown that the time between events has an exponential distribution. Furthermore, the probability that we observe k events in an interval of length t is given by: P[k events in interval of length t]  =   (λt) k _ k !  e −λt. (14) In finance and investment management, the Poisson distribution is particularly use­ ful for modeling the frequency of discrete, rare events over a specific period, such as the number of defaults in a loan portfolio, the arrival rate of orders in a trading system during different scenarios, or the timing of inflows and outflows in liquidity management models.

Predicting Corporate Default To assess credit risk in corporate bond portfolios, there are different approaches to quantify the risk of default. Such credit risk models are either structural models or reduced form models. Structural models assume that a company would default if its assets are worth less than its liabilities. These models calculate the firm’s probability of default based on the evolution of the value of its assets and liabilities. Reduced form models assume that default is caused by external factors and model it as a random event, independent of the firm’s balance sheet. This ran­ dom default event is often described using a Poisson process, which focuses on the arrival rate or intensity of default. This approach is also known as default intensity modeling and estimates the probability of no default (or no events) from time 0 to t as: P(No default)  =  e −λ×t.

The expected time until the first and only default is: E[t d]  =   1 _ λ . Assume the intensity of default, λ, or hazard rate, for a particular corporate bond is 0.02 per year. To simulate any other distribution, first we simulate outcomes from a uniform distribution and then use the inverse of the CDF for the target dis­ tribution to obtain a random value. In this way, uniform distributions facilitate large-scale Monte Carlo simulation, a computational method that uses repeated random sampling to estimate the behavior and outcomes of a complex system or process. Typically, a random number is drawn from a uniform distribution, which is then transformed into a random draw from another distribution. For example, if we wanted to simulate from the previously dis­ cussed distribution of the sum of two dice, we start by drawing from a uniform distri­ bution between 0 and 1 and then use the CDF for the target distribution to determine the random draw from our target distribution. Say we draw 0.333; this would imply a result of 6 for the draw from the two-dice distribution, because 0.333 is between the bounds of 0.2778 and 0.4167 for the CDF, as seen in Exhibit 5. These simulations model possible results using a relevant distribution for any vari­ able with inherent uncertainty, recalculating the results multiple times with different random numbers drawn from a specific range. This process is repeated thousands of times, producing a variety of possible outcomes. The complete simulation provides a range of possible outcomes, each with its associated probability. This approach can predict asset price paths, offering a likely range of asset values with equal probability. The following case study shows an example, and we will discuss Monte Carlo simu­ lations later in the curriculum.

Monte Carlo Simulation of Stock Prices To conduct a Monte Carlo simulation for predicting stock prices, the parameters of the simulation must first be defined. We first draw from the uniform distri­ bution random values between 0 and 1. That random number is then mapped to the inverse of the target distribution’s CDF, a point on the cumulative dis­ tribution corresponding to that value. This random number defines the point on the cumulative density distribution and helps generate the price paths. For stock prices, this target distribution is often the normal distribution, due to the assumption of log-normal returns. Following this, multiple simulated paths for the stock price are generated, and the results are interpreted. The following example illustrates 100 individual Monte Carlo simulation paths modeled using the Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM) formula: S t  =  S 0 e (μ− σ 2 _ 2 )t+σW t, where S t is the price at time t S 0 is the initial price, or 10 μ is the average annual return of 10% σ 2 is the annual variance 0.04, equivalent to a standard deviation, σ, of 20% t is the time W t is a random component known as a Brownian motion and can be thought of as the noise where the changes are distributed normally. This formula accounts for both the deterministic trend—drift—and the random fluctuations—volatility—of the stock price. The random component has a discrete value for each specific incremental time period. The deterministic trend, or drift, is μ −  σ 2 _ 2 ; it represents the expected return of the stock minus half the variance and provides a smooth, predictable trend over time.

Key Statistical Distributions in Finance The random fluctuations flow from the σ W t term. Here, σ is the standard deviation and measures volatility; W t is a Wiener process or Brownian motion that introduces randomness, which here is normally distributed noise with a mean of zero and a standard deviation of 1. As an example of how to perform a simulation step, assume the time step is one day. Since a typical trading year has 250 days, the time increment t in the formula will be  1 _ . The steps are as follows: Step 1: Draw a random value from a uniform distribution [0,1]. For instance, let’s say the random value drawn is 0.07. Step 2: Convert the uniform random value into a normal value. Using the CDF of a standard normal distribution N(0, 1), determine the point where 0.07 falls in the normal distribution. For this example, we find that 0.07 corresponds to approximately −1.48 in the standard normal distribution. Step 3: Use the result from Step 2 as W t in the GBM formula. Substitute the value of W t  =  − 1.48 into the formula for S t: S 1  =  S 0 e (μ− σ 2 _ 2 )t+σW t. For example, this might yield S 1  =  9.818. Step 4: Continue the process for each time step to simulate the entire path of the asset price over time. Using these parameters, 100 stock price paths over the 250-day time horizon are simulated. Each path represents one potential future trajectory of the stock price, and Exhibit 14 visualizes the evolution of each of these 10 paths and the range of potential outcomes. Exhibit 14: Monte Carlo Simulation Stock Price Paths Trading Days Stock Price The average simulated final price is 11.09, implying an 11.09% return predicted by the model based on the given assumptions about the initial price, return, and standard deviation. Within the simulation, the mean of the return will drive the mean of the simulation paths. This relationship manifests as the drift upward in the average across trading days. The standard deviation drives the divergence or “spreading out” of the paths from the starting point.

It is a cornerstone of statistical analysis. Many independent random variables, or sums of them, tend toward a normal distribution even if the original variables themselves are not normally distributed. Consider the sum of a large number of independent Bernoulli trials with p = ½ will converge to a normal distribution as the number of trials increase. As such, normal distribution is widely used in risk management. Binomial distributions converge to normal distributions, as previously shown. The normal distribution is fully defined by the mean μ and the variance σ 2 and is denoted as N(μ, σ 2); it is symmetric about its mean, so that the mode and the median are the same. Its skewness is 0, its kurtosis is 3, and excess kurtosis is 0. Exhibit 15 shows a standard normal distribution, a special case of the normal distribution with μ = 0 and σ 2  =  1. Log-Normal Distribution: Modeling non-negative outcomes A random variable has a log-normal distribution if its logarithm is normally distrib­ uted; thus, the variable is positively skewed and can take only positive values. In finance and investments, the log-normal distribution is particularly useful for modeling prices of stocks since prices cannot fall below zero and often exhibit skewed distributions. The Black–Scholes option pricing model assumes that stock prices are log-normally distributed and that log returns, ln  S 1 / S 0  =  ln[S 1] − ln[S 0], are normally distributed. Using logarithmic returns enhances the accuracy in financial modeling over time. Simple returns, calculated as the percentage change between consecutive prices, P 1 / P 0 − 1, assume normal distribution but can be unrealistic since they allow values below −100%, which isn’t possible because prices cannot fall below zero. Logarithmic returns, on the other hand, use the natural logarithm of the price ratio, ln  P 1 / P 0, and are bounded, making them additive and more appropriate for longer periods. Simple returns are not additive across multiple periods. Log returns are additive, reflect continuous compounding, and are more suited for models with long time horizons, where simple returns may misestimate total returns and volatility. Simple returns are useful for short-term interpretations, but log returns are usually used for complex analysis because they are more accurate in handling long-term volatility in financial data. The product of independent log-normally distributed variables is also log-normally distributed, aligning with how returns compound over time.

Logistic Distribution The logistic distribution is a continuous probability distribution characterized by a symmetric, S-shaped CDF, used in logistic regression and neural networks, defined by its location and scale parameters. It is typically used for modeling growth processes. Logistic regression is used for binary classification problems, where the outcome variable has two possible categories, such as “success” or “failure.” It models the prob­ ability of one category occurring, making it ideal for predicting binary outcomes. On the other hand, the Poisson regression is used for modeling discrete count data, where the outcome variable represents the number of times an event occurs within a given time period, and is typically used to predict event frequencies. In finance and investments, the logistic distribution is central to logistic regression, a statistical method for analyzing datasets in which there are one or more independent variables that determine a binary outcome. The logistic distribution is also widely used for machine learning and artificial intelligence. The logistic distribution resembles the normal distribution in shape but has heavier tails. This distribution is defined by the location parameter μ, which is also the mean, and the scale parameter s, which is related to its variance. Conditional Expectations, Variances, and Covariances Joint Distributions of Random Variables Joint distributions allow for examining the simultaneous distribution of two random variables. Understanding the joint distribution of asset returns helps investors assess the degree of correlation, or dependence between asset returns, which is essential for effective diversification and risk management The joint bivariate CDF, F 12(x 1, x 2), quantifies the likelihood that the random vari­ able X 1 will not exceed a specific value x 1 and that simultaneously, X 2 will not exceed x 2. Mathematically, where P denotes the probability of the event occurring, this is expressed as: F 12(x 1, x 2)  =  P(X 1  ≤  x 1, X 2  ≤  x 2). (22) The three-dimensional surface plot in Exhibit 21 captures this definition by visually depicting the function, F 12(x 1, x 2), which signifies the joint probability that both X 1 and X 2 will assume values at or below x 1 and x 2, respectively. Exhibit 21: Joint Probability Density 0.20 0.15 0.10 F12(U1, U2) X2 X1 0.05 0.00 –5 –4 –3 –2 –1 –5 –3 –1 0.00–0.05 0.05–0.10 0.10–0.15 0.15–0.20 The height of the surface at any point (x 1, x 2) is proportional to the joint PDF f 12 (x , x 2 ). Peaks on this plot signal areas of higher probability density, implying a greater likelihood of occurrence for the corresponding values of X 1and X 2. The visual rep­ resentation illustrates the relationship between continuous random variables f 12(u , u 2) over the entire range of possible values, typically bounded by − ∞ and ∞, and is proportional to the probability that X 1 and X 2 fall within a small interval around the point (x 1, x 2). For the two continuous random variables, X 1 and X 2, the joint distribution over the entire possible range can be found by integrating the joint PDF: F 12(x 1, x 2)  =  ∫ −∞ x ∫ −∞ x f 12(u 1, u 2)d u 1 d u 2. (23) Equation 23 is the joint density function. When the variables in question are indepen­ dent of each other, the joint density function is simply the product of the individual densities of each variable, expressed as: f 12(u 1, u 2)  =  f 1(u 1) × f 2(u 2). (24)

Statistical Distributions for Financial Asset Prices and Returns Color gradations in Exhibit 21 delineate various probability densities, aiding in under­ standing the distribution’s spread and density across the range of X 1 and X 2. The joint distribution function can be simplified to: F 12(x 1, x 2)  =  F 1(x 1) × F 2(x 2)  =  P(X 1  ≤  x 1) × P(X 2  ≤  x 2). To isolate the behavior of one variable from another, we turn to marginal densities. Marginal density is the probability distribution of a single variable within a multivar­ iate distribution and isolates a single variable’s distribution from a set of variables that are otherwise interconnected. It is obtained by integrating the joint density function over the range of the other variable(s). Because the marginal density provides the distribution of a single variable in iso­ lation, extracted from the joint distribution of multiple variables, it allows for under­ standing the features of the variable in isolation. For an investor managing a portfolio, understanding the features of the variable in isolation is particularly important when an investor is interested in the performance of only one asset within a portfolio. It can be used to manage its risk or assess its performance independent from other assets in the portfolio, but within the context of the portfolio. In our bivariate example, we can obtain the marginal density of X 1 by integrating f 12(x 1, u 2) over u 2: f X 1(x 1)  =    ∫ −∞ ∞ f X 1X 2(x 1, u 2) d u 2. (25) Equation 25 integrates the joint density function over all possible values of u 2, resulting in a density function that exclusively depends on X 1. Similarly, for the other dimension: f X 2(x 2)  =  ∫ −∞ ∞ f X 1X 2(u 1, x 2) d u 1. (26) Equation 26 integrates the joint density function over all possible values of u 1, resulting in a density function that exclusively depends on X 2 (i.e., other variables and their impact and influence have been removed). The principles of joint and marginal distributions are represented differently for discrete variables, typically in the form of a contingency table, a tabular represen­ tation that summarizes the relationship between several categorical variables by displaying the frequencies at which certain combinations of categories occur, rather than a continuous surface plot.

Conditional Expectations The conditional expectation, denoted as E[XY  =  y], represents the expected value of a random variable X given that another random variable Y is equal to y, Y  =  y. This definition extends to more general conditions, not just equality, and provides a way to update our expectations based on new information. For example, when conducting scenario analysis in a portfolio context, understanding the conditional expectation allows investors to evaluate how the potential returns, r x, on one asset, X, are influ­ enced when another asset, Y, has a known return, r y. The calculation of the conditional PDF of X given Y  =  y depends on whether the variables are discretely or continuously distributed.
•  For discrete variables, it involves summing over the possible values of X, weighted by their conditional probabilities, given Y  =  y: E[XY  =  y]  =  ∑ x  x × P(X  =  x|Y  =  y). (27)
•  For continuous variables, the calculation involves an integral over the possi­ ble values of X, weighted by their conditional PDFs: E[XY  =  y]  =  ∫ x × f X|Y(x|y)dx. (28)
•  The expected variance is: Var(X|Y  =  y)  =  E[(X − E[X|Y  =  y]) 2|Y  =  y] = E[X 2|Y  =  y] − (E[X|Y  =  y]) 2. (29)

Conditional Expectations, Variances, and Covariances Conditional Means, Variances, and Covariances Conditional measures provide an understanding of the data under certain assumptions and conditions.

•  The conditional mean is the expected value of a random variable given that a certain condition is true. Mathematically, this relationship involves the value of a random variable X, assuming it is dependent on a specific condi­ tion, S, being met: E[X|S]  =  ∑ i=1 n  X i × P(X i |S). (31) The expected value of X, given S, calculated by summing the products of each possible outcome of X and its conditional probability, given S, shows that expectations can change when information about specific scenarios is incorporated.
•  The conditional variance measures the dispersion of a random variable around its conditional mean, calculated as: Var(X|S)  =  E[(X − E[X|S]) 2]. (32)

•  The conditional covariance measures how two variables co-move under the given condition. It is calculated similarly to unconditional covariance, but under the given condition, or: Cov((X|S), (Y|S))  =  E[(X − E[(X|S)])(Y − E[(Y|S)])]| . (33)

formulate investment problems through Bayesian updating Forecasting the future is hard; “forecasting” history is easier. The difficulty in fore­ casting stems not only from the unpredictability of the future but also from the complexity of integrating diverse information into coherent and hopefully reasonably unbiased predictions. Extracting meaningful information from noisy data is difficult. Predicting future outcomes is challenging. Cognitive myopia may lead us to discard contradictory information. The goal of modeling the behavior of markets, prices, and returns is to develop a set of possible future outcomes and their associated probabilities. These outcomes and their probabilities can then be consistently revised in response to the arrival of new information. Thoughtfully designed financial models allow analysts to update and improve their forecasts over time. Probability trees and Bayesian updating of expec­ tations and probabilities bring together powerful concepts that support economic forecasting, asset valuation, and portfolio allocation. Bayes’ theorem, also known as Bayes’ rule or Bayes’ formula, is a core concept in probability theory and statistics that describes how to update the probabilities of hypotheses in light of additional data, thereby enhancing decision-making accuracy.

•  A priori probability, or prior probability, is the probability of an event or hypothesis before considering new data. It reflects pre-existing beliefs based on prior knowledge and past observations. This is an ex-ante probability.

•  A posteriori probability, or posterior probability, is the probability of an event or hypothesis after incorporating data from new evidence, events, or observations. This conditional probability is derived using Bayes’ theorem, which updates the prior probabilities to reflect the new data. This is an ex-post probability. Bayes’ theorem works in reverse to the total probability rule, P(A)  =  ∑ n  P(A ∩ B n). It decomposes the probability of an event based on the intersection with other events and their respective probabilities. While the idea of using new information to update estimates of probabilities is intuitive, its formal statement can be difficult to follow. An easy way to both remember and derive Bayes’ theorem is to look at the probability of the intersection of two events, A and B. It should be trivially clear that the probability of both Events A and B occurring is equal to the probability of both Events B and A occurring, P(A ∩ B)  =  P(B ∩ A). Accordingly, the probability P(A ∩ B)  =  P(A|B)P(B) (i.e., the conditional probability that Event A given Event B occurs times the probability that Event B occurs). Similarly, the probability P(B ∩ A)  =  P(B|A)P(A) (i.e., the conditional probability that Event B given Event A occurs times the probability that Event A occurs). Formally: P(A|B)P(B)  =  P(A ∩ B)  =  P(B ∩ A)  =  P(B|A)P(A). (34)
Bayesian Updating Rearranging the outermost expressions yields Bayes’ theorem: P(A|B)  = P(B|A)P(A) _ P(B)  , (35) where
P(A|B) is the posterior probability of A occurring given that B is true
P(B|A) is the conditional probability of B given A is true
P(A) is the prior probability of observing A

P(B) is the marginal probability of observing B Updating beliefs about the potential causes of a new observation allows us to refine the prior probabilities for an event of interest upon receiving new information. It is important to note that the theorem is applicable to both discrete and continuous random variables. The following case study conceptualizes Bayes’ formula from the perspective of marginal probabilities.

Stock Market Returns and Technology Companies Previously, we analyzed the contingency table for a large-cap stock index: The index consists of 500 firms, 100 of which are technology firms. Among these, 60 firms experienced returns exceeding 10%, while 40 had returns of 10% or less. Conversely, of the 400 non-technology firms, 100 had returns over 10%, and 300 had returns of 10% or less. The earlier Exhibit 21 is shown here as Exhibit 28. The last row and the last column are the marginal distributions of the rate of return and the type of firm, respectively. The marginal probabilities give the overall distribution of each variable, not considering the other variable. For example, the probability of randomly selecting a firm from this sample of 500 firms that is non-technology is 80 %   =   400 _ . From Exhibit 28, we can find the probability that a firm is a tech firm given that the return is > 10% or P(Tech|R  >  10%). Exhibit 26 provides the following inferred, empirical probabilities:

Bayes’ formula calculates the probability that a firm has a return of > 10%, R > 10%, and then the probability that a firm with a return of > 10% is a tech firm, P(Tech firm|R  >  10%). First, P(R  >  10%) =  P(R  >  10% | Tech firm) × P(Tech firm) + P(R  >  10 % |Non-tech firm) × P(Non-tech firm) = 0.60 × 0.20 + 0.25 × 0.80 = 0.32. P(R  >  10%) =  0.60 × 0.20 _ 0.32   =  0.375. This result indicates an increased likelihood of a firm being a tech firm, given it has a return greater than 10%, compared to the overall probability of a firm being a tech firm in the sample, which is 0.20. With underlying probability models with assumed distributions, the updating here concerns the true probabilities, given that certain paths have been taken or certain events have occurred.

Sustainability Investments as a Predictor of Earnings Expectations EcoMed A/S, a leading generic pharmaceutical manufacturer, will release its annual earnings next week. The market typically reacts positively if a company’s earnings per share (EPS) exceed consensus estimates and negatively if they fall short. EcoMed A/S investors face three mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive earnings outcomes:
•  Exceeded consensus estimates
•  Met consensus estimates

•  Fell short of consensus estimates Before receiving any new information, the following priors are formulated: P(EPS exceeded consensus)  =  0.45 P(EPS met consensus)  =  0.30 P(EPS fell short of consensus)  =  0.25 Before earnings are released, EcoMed A/S reveals its investments in sustainable practices across its facilities in Germany and Brazil, aiming to reduce its car­ bon footprint and enhance its renewable energy usage due to increased oper­ ational demands. This development suggests stronger-than-expected financial

Bayesian Updating performance, as expanding sustainable practices often correlates with robust sales and improved profitability, which in turn could imply that EcoMed A/S EPS exceeded consensus estimates. To adjust earnings expectations, using the Bayesian methodology, we can adjust to new information. Based on similar events in comparable industries, the likelihood of these climate-based sustainable expansions under each EPS scenario can be estimated as:
•  P(EcoMed invests in sustainability|EPS exceeded consensus)  =  0.75
•  P(EcoMed invests in sustainability|EPS met consensus)  =  0.20

•  P(EcoMed invests in sustainability|EPS fell short of consensus)  =  0.05 With these three updated conditional probabilities, and using the total probability rule, the unconditional probability of EcoMed A/S investing in sustainability is: P(EcoMed invests in sustainability)  =  0.75 × 0.45 + 0.20 × 0.30 + 0.05 × 0.25 =  0.41. To find the updated probability that EcoMed A/S EPS would exceed consensus estimates given the new investments in sustainability, using Bayes’ formula: P(EPS exceeded consensus|EcoMed invests in sustainability) = P(EcoMed invests in sustainability|EPS exceeded consensus) × P(EPS exceeded consensus)

P(EcoMed invests in sustainability) =  0.75 × 0.45 _ 0.41   =  0.823. The a priori likelihood that EcoMed A/S would outperform consensus EPS expectations was 45%. After analyzing the company’s commitment to sustain­ ability, this probability has been revised to 82.3%, reflecting an updated, more confident belief, considering the new information. The case study recalibrated the priors using new information:
•  The denominator, P(EcoMed invests in sustainability), represents the over­ all probability of investment into sustainability without any conditioning information.

•  The numerator, (EcoMed invests in sustainability|EPS exceeded consen­ sus) × P(EPS exceeded consensus), specifically accounts for the scenario where last quarter’s EPS exceeded consensus estimates. The new data have effectively increased the likelihood of outperforming EPS expectations, thus altering prior beliefs to form new, updated probabilities.

Sustainability Investments as a Predictor of Earnings Expectations Recall the updated probability that last quarter’s EPS exceeded the consensus estimate from 45% to 82.3% after EcoMed A/S announced it would invest in environmentally sustainable production.

Statistical Distributions for Financial Asset Prices and Returns 1.	 What is the probability that EcoMed met consensus estimates, given the investment in sustainability? Solution: The probability is P(EPS met consensus|EcoMed invests in sustainability) = P(EcoMed invests in sustainability|EPS met consensus)

P(EcoMed invests in sustainability)    × P(EPS met consensus). The probability P(EcoMed invests in sustainability ) is found by taking each of the three conditional probabilities in the statement of the problem, such as P(EcoMed invests in sustainability |EPS exceeded consensus); multiply­ ing each one by the prior probability of the conditioning event, such as P (EPS exceeded consensus); and then adding the three products. The calculation is unchanged from the problem above: P(EcoMed in­ vests in sustainability)  =  0.75(0.45) + 0.20(0.30) + 0.05(0.25)  =  0.41, or 41%. The other probabilities needed, P(EcoMed invests in sustainabili­ ty |EPS met consensus)  =  0.20 and P(EPS met consensus)  =  0.30, are givens; hence: P(EPS met consensus|EcoMed invests in sustainability) = P(EcoMed invests in sustainability|EPS met consensus)

P(EcoMed invests in sustainability)    × P(EPS met consensus) =  0.20 _ 0.41 × 0.30  =  0.4878(0.30)  =  0.1463. After taking account of the announcement on sustainability investments, the updated probability that last quarter’s EPS for EcoMed A/S just met consen­ sus is 14.63% compared with the prior probability of 30%. 2.	 Update the prior probability that EcoMed A/S EPS fell short of consensus. Solution: P(EcoMed invests in sustainability) was already calculated as 41%. Recall that P(EcoMed invests in sustainability |EPS fell short of consensus)  =  0.05 and P(EPS fell short of consensus)  =  0.25 are given. P(EPS fell short of consensus|EcoMed invests in sustainability) = P(EcoMed invests in sustainability|EPS fell short of consensus)

P(EcoMed invests in sustainability) × P(EPS fell short of consensus) =  0.05 _ 0.41 × 0.25  =  0.1219(0.25)  =  0.03048. As a result of the announcement, the revised probability that EcoMed A/S EPS fell short of consensus decreases from 25% prior to 3% posterior. 3.	 Show that the three updated probabilities sum to 1. Solution: The sum of the three updated probabilities is:

Bayesian Updating P(EPS exceeded consensus|EcoMed invests in sustainability) + P(EPS met consensus|EcoMed invests in sustainability) + P(EPS fell short of consensus|EcoMed invests in sustainability) = 0.8232 + 0.1463 + 0.0305  =  1.0000. The three events (EPS exceeded consensus, EPS met consensus, EPS fell short of consensus) are mutually exclusive and exhaustive: One of these events or statements must be true, so the conditional probabilities must sum to 1. Whether probabilities are conditional or unconditional, whenever we have a complete set of distinct possible events or outcomes, the probabilities must sum to 1. When the prior probabilities are equal, the probability of information given an event equals the probability of the event given the information. When a decision maker has equal prior probabilities, or diffuse prior, the probability of an event is determined by the information.

A.	 0.10 B.	 0.47 C.	 0.72 Solution: The correct response is A. The equation using the total probability rule: P(passes test)  =  P(passes test|survivor)P(survivor) + P(passes test|non-survivor)P(non-survivor). We know that P(survivor)  =  1 − P(non-survivor)  =  1 − 0.40  =  0.60. Therefore, P(passes test)  =  0.55  =  0.85(0.60) + P(passes test|non-survivor) (0.40). Thus, P(passes test|non-survivor)  =   0.55 − (0.85 × 0.60)

Alternative C is incorrect: P(non-survivor) / P(pass­ es test)  =  0.40 / 0.55  =  0.72. 3.	 What is the probability that a company will fail the test, given it is a non-survivor, P(fails test|non-survivor)? A.	 0.10 B.	 0.53 C.	 0.90 Solution: The correct response is C. The probability that a company fails the test given it is a non-survivor can be found by taking the complement of the prob­ ability that it passes the test under the same condition. Because P(pass­ es test|non-survivor)  =  0.10, the complement, P(fails test|non-survivor), is 1 − P(passes test|non-survivor)  =  1 − 0.10  =  0.90. blocks.x: •  Random variables represent numerical outcomes of a random experiment and can be discrete, countable, continuous, or uncountable.
•  The probability mass function, PMF, for discrete variables shows the proba­ bility of each value.
•  The probability density function, PDF, for continuous variables is propor­ tional to the probability of observing a particular value in a small interval around any value.
•  The cumulative distribution function, CDF, gives the probability that a ran­ dom variable is less than or equal to a specific value.
•  The expected value is the weighted average of the numerical outcomes of a random variable weighted by its PMF or PDF.
•  The unconditional expectation represents the average outcome of random variables.
•  The moments of a distribution are the unconditional expectations of ran­ dom variables.
•  The joint density of two random variables describes the probability distribu­ tion of all possible simultaneous occurrences of pairs of outcomes.
•  Marginal probability distributions isolate the distribution of a single random variable, independent of others with which they are jointly distributed.
•  Conditional distributions focus on the distribution of a random variable given the values of other random variables with which it shares a joint distribution.
•  Conditional expectations represent the expected value of a random variable under certain conditions using the appropriate conditional distribution.
•  Probability trees visualize the likelihood of various outcomes.
•  Bayes’ theorem updates probabilities with new evidence, quantifying the likelihood of certain outcomes, given the new information.

blocks.x: TESTING This learning module explores the application of hypothesis tests, a foundational sta­ tistical method used in finance to evaluate assumptions about population parameters such as returns, variances, and correlations. Hypothesis testing is crucial to developing investment strategies, analyzing portfolio performance, and assessing risk. First, we examine the central limit theorem, confidence intervals, and various sam­ pling methodologies. Next, we introduce hypothesis testing and discuss its applications in finance. We conclude by comparing and contrasting parametric and non-parametric tests, including the underlying assumptions and practical uses.
