C is incorrect because rebalancing changes the portfolio’s asset mix, which affects returns when assets perform differently.
The Minimum–Variance Portfolio and the Efficient Frontier

sections.title: The Minimum–Variance Portfolio And The Efficient Frontier

blocks.x: describe, calculate, and interpret the minimum-variance portfolio and portfolios that lie on the efficient frontier Portfolio optimization entails finding the optimal mix of assets in a portfolio, subject to certain given constraints, such as required return or maximum risk. Given the set of available risky assets and any constraints that might be in place, we can create feasible portfolios that meet these constraints. Exhibit 13 plots the risk and return of 10,000 randomly generated feasible portfolios, each having 10 assets. Unlike the feasible portfolios for the two-asset case, which can be seen to lie on a curve in Exhibit 3, these feasible portfolios occupy a region in risk–return space and offer a wide range of risk and return characteristics. Exhibit 13: Feasible Portfolios and Their Risk and Return Feasible Portfolios Standard Deviation of Returns, Risk, % Returns, % Each portfolio here is a risky portfolio, a collection of assets with an uncertain return, exposing investors to potential gains or losses. The scatterplot visualizes the wide range of possible trade-offs between risk and return: Some higher risk portfolios, especially those portfolios on the upper boundary of the cloud of feasible portfolios in Exhibit 13, offer higher expected returns than portfolios below the upper boundary. However, this relationship is not linear, indicating the diminishing marginal returns of taking on additional risk. For any given level of risk, some portfolios have higher expected returns than others, suggesting that they are closer to being optimal in terms of their risk–return trade-off than other portfolios that lie below them on the plot.

The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio To identify these optimal portfolios, we introduce the Markowitz efficient frontier, or simply efficient frontier. Portfolios on this frontier are considered optimal because they maximize expected return for each level of risk. Equivalently, they minimize risk for any given level of expected return. In Exhibit 13, the efficient frontier can be visualized as the upper boundary of the cloud of feasible portfolios The availability of a wide range of risk–return trade-offs allows investors to tailor their portfolios to match their preferences, as well as to include their preferred portfolio constraints when constructing them. Portfolios whose mean and standard deviation are above and left of the efficient frontier cannot be constructed using the available set of assets. Portfolio constraints typically include restrictions on assets that can be held, minimum or maximum investment amounts of individual assets and sectors, and non-negative weights. The impacts of such constraints on portfolio selection and portfolio management are discussed throughout the curriculum. Mathematically, the portfolio optimization problem is generally formulated as:
Minimize   σ P =  ∑ i=1 N  ∑ j=1 N  w i w j σ i,j
subject to ∑ i=1 N  w i  =  1, w i  ≥  0
and E [ r P ] = k (22) where

k = a constant value from the feasible set of returns for this particular set of investment options. Because w i  ≥  0 and ∑ i=1 N  w i  =  1, the feasible set of portfolio returns k must lie between the minimum and maximum of the individual asset returns: min i (E[r i])  ≤  k  ≤  max i (E[r i]). Thus, both the minimum and maximum feasible values of k are constrained by the returns of investable assets. The goal of optimization is to minimize the portfolio variance for the given target return k, subject to the constraint that the sum of the individual portfolio asset weights equals one and with no allowance for negative weights. The condition w i  ≥  0 is a no-short-selling constraint. Short selling is a strategy in which an investor borrows and sells a security, anticipating its price will drop. Later, the investor buys back the security at a lower price to return it to the lender, profiting from the price decline if the security was indeed overvalued. Short selling can be seen as speculative, but it can also be used to hedge the downside risk of a long position. We will discuss short selling in more detail throughout the curriculum. Equation 22 can be expressed compactly in terms of matrices and vectors, as: Minimize σ P =  w T Vw subject to w T 1  =  1, w T r  =  k, w  ≥  0, where w = the vector of asset weights w T = the transpose of the vector of asset weights r = the vector of returns for the assets V = the covariance matrix of the assets w T Vw = the matrix form representation of the portfolio variance expres­ sion, or

The Minimum–Variance Portfolio and the Efficient Frontier σ P =  ∑ i=1 N  ∑ j=1 N  w i w j σ i,j w T 1  =  1 = the matrix for summing the weights of the assets in the portfolio to one, or ∑ i=1 N  w i  =  1 w  ≥  0 = an expression that imposes the condition that no short selling is allowed Note: Contents of this shaded box are not examinable material. Solving a portfolio-optimization problem with more than two assets would require extensive mathematical manipulation using matrix algebra, quadratic programming, or numerical optimization approaches, which are outside of the scope of this learning module. Because the focus here is on a portfolio with two assets, we can derive the results without matrix algebra or complicated optimization. These findings for the two-asset portfolio case can be generalized to a portfolio of any number of assets. The Minimum-Variance Portfolio The minimum-variance portfolio is the portfolio that exhibits the lowest possible variance among all feasible portfolios. Exhibit 14 shows the set of feasible portfolios from Exhibit 13 with the minimum-variance portfolio identified with a red dot. Exhibit 14: The Minimum-Variance Portfolio and the Feasible Portfolios Returns, % Minimum Variance Portfolio Max Return Min Return Standard Deviation of Returns, Risk, % Minimum Variance Portfolio: Return: 9.87%; Standard Deviation: 13.36% Minimum Return Portfolio: Return: 4.17%; Standard Deviation: 17.65% Maximum Return Portfolio: Return: 14.79%; Standard Deviation: 17.42% Min Variance The minimum-variance portfolio has the lowest risk, measured by standard deviation, among all feasible portfolios. It offers a return of 9.87% and a standard deviation of 13.36%. For comparison, the maximum-return portfolio, identified with a green dot, offers a return of 14.79% and a standard deviation of 17.42%. The minimum-return portfolio, located at the lowest point on the y-axis and identified with an orange dot, offers a return of 4.17% and a standard deviation of 17.65%. Despite having a similar

The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio risk level, the return for the minimum-return portfolio is significantly lower than that of the maximum-return portfolio, nicely illustrating the importance of portfolio composition. The least risky portfolio that can be constructed from a given set of assets is the minimum-variance portfolio. This portfolio serves as the foundation for the construction of the efficient frontier. Exhibit 15 shows the feasible portfolios, the minimum-variance portfolio, and the Markowitz efficient frontier. Exhibit 15: The Efficient Frontier and the Minimum-Variance Portfolio with all the Feasible Portfolios Standard Deviation of Returns, Risk, % Returns, % Minimum Variance Portfolio: Return: 9.87%; Standard Deviation: 13.36% Efficient Frontier Minimum Variance Portfolio Investors should choose portfolios along the efficient frontier, which offers the best pos­ sible return for each level of risk. The frontier spans from the global minimum-variance portfolio, the leftmost point with the lowest variance, and upward and rightward to portfolios with higher expected returns and volatility. When a risk‐free asset is available, the optimal risky portfolio (often called the tangency portfolio) is the one on the efficient frontier that maximizes the Sharpe ratio. The minimum‐variance portfolio remains the leftmost point on the frontier, while the tangency portfolio is the single “optimal” risky‐asset combination combining the risk‐free asset to achieve the highest risk‐adjusted return. To illustrate these ideas, we turn to a two‐asset example. Analyzing just two assets makes it simpler to identify the minimum‐variance and tangency portfolios on a risk–return (standard deviation vs. expected return) diagram. Here, the Sharpe ratio naturally appears when we introduce a risk‐free asset and seek a point of tangency on the two‐asset frontier. Although the full efficient frontier can include many assets, the two‐asset case illustrates how portfolio weights, variance, and covariance combine to determine risk and return. Before finding the optimal risky portfolio, we first calculate the minimum‐variance portfolio. Consider a portfolio consisting of two assets with weights w A and w B, respectively, which must sum to one: w A + w B  =  1, and the portfolio weights must be non-negative: w A, w B  ≥  0.
The Minimum–Variance Portfolio and the Efficient Frontier The portfolio variance, σ p 2, is expressed as: σ P =  w A σ A + w B σ B + 2 w A w B σ A,B, where
σ A = the variance of returns for Asset A
σ B = the variance of returns for Asset B

σ A,B = the covariance between the returns of Assets A and B Using the constraint that the weights sum to one, we can express w B as: w B  =  1 − w A. Substituting w B  =  1 − w A into the variance equation, we get: σ P =  w A σ A + (1 − w A) 2 σ B + 2 w A(1 − w A) σ A,B σ P =  w A (σ A + σ B − 2 σ A,B) + 2 w A(σ A,B − σ B ) + σ B . To find the minimum variance, we take the derivative of σ p 2 with respect to w A and set it to zero:
d σ P

_ d w A =  2 w A(σ A + σ B − 2 σ A,B) + 2(σ A,B − σ B )  =  0. This step achieves two objectives. First, taking the derivative of σ p 2 with respect to w A calculates the incremental change in portfolio variance for an incremental change in the weight of Asset A. Second, by imposing

d σ p 2 _ d w A =  0, we know we have come to the point on the plot of variance versus w A where the tangent line is flat, indicating either a maximum, minimum, or saddle point. We can show that if w A is less than the w A that satisfies this equation, then the variance is decreasing, and if it is greater the variance is increasing. Therefore, we are at a min­ imum. Simplifying the above yields: w A(σ A + σ B − 2 σ A,B)  =  σ B − σ A,B.
Then, rearranging to solve for w A: w A  = σ B − σ A,B ____________
σ A + σ B − 2 σ A,B , (23) and for w B: w B  =  1 − w A  =  1 − σ B − σ A,B ____________

σ A + σ B − 2 σ A,B . (24) These weights minimize the portfolio’s variance and provide the foundation for con­ structing the minimum-variance frontier for the two-asset case, which we discuss later in this section. The minimum-variance portfolio return is not a consideration: The only objective is to minimize the portfolio variance. This approach is also one of the building blocks for optimizing portfolios with more than two assets. Readers without a knowledge of calculus can easily verify this result in a spreadsheet. By setting up cells for w 1, w 2  =  1 − w 1, σ A , σ B 2, and σ A,B, the variance of the portfolio can be computed using Equation 11. The solver can then be used to find the optimal weights, which can be compared to those obtained from Equation 23 and Equation 24.

The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio To calculate the optimal risky portfolio, we start by inserting the expected returns for each asset, E[r A] and E[r B], into the equation for the expected return of the port­ folio, E[r P]. The portfolio that maximizes the Sharpe ratio—the ratio of the Expected Return less the risk-free rate to the standard deviation—is the optimal risky portfolio. Accordingly, we can utilize the same procedure we employed to find the minimum variance portfolio but this time we are trying to maximize the Sharpe Ratio. We will discuss the Sharpe ratio later in the learning module. For portfolios with more than two assets, this process extends by generalizing the weights, variances, and covariances to include all assets, often solved using numerical optimization techniques.

The Minimum–Variance Portfolio and the Efficient Frontier
Exhibit 16: The Minimum-Variance Portfolio and the Minimum- Variance Frontier

Standard Deviation of Portfolio Return (%) Portfolio Return (%) Minimum-Variance Frontier Minimum-Variance Portfolio S&P 500 MSCI EM Minimum – Variance Portfolio: S&P 500 Weight: 80.79% MSCI EM Weight: 19.21% Return: 11.52% Risk: 14.59% Exhibit 16 illustrates various points. An investor who seeks high returns and is willing to take on more risk will opt for a portfolio further to the upper right of the efficient frontier. Likewise, an investor who prefers lower risk will choose a portfolio that lies closer to the lower left of the efficient frontier. And an inves­ tor who wants a balance of risk and return will choose a portfolio around the center of the efficient frontier. The segment of the curved line that lies below the minimum-variance portfolio is not used, as there are portfolios on the efficient frontier that offer a higher expected return for the same level of risk. Finally, Exhibit 16 shows the benefit of diversification: Combining different assets can reduce portfolio risk at any given level of expected return, particularly if the assets are negatively or weakly correlated. In other words a combination of two risky assets can be less risky than either of them.
Knowledge Check

1.	 The portfolio on the minimum-variance frontier with the lowest standard deviation is the: A.	 optimal risky portfolio. B.	 portfolio with the highest return. C.	 global minimum-variance portfolio. Solution: The correct answer is C. The global minimum-variance portfolio is the port­ folio on the minimum-variance frontier with the lowest standard deviation. Although the portfolio is attainable, when the risk-free asset is considered, the global minimum-variance portfolio is not the optimal risky portfolio. Alternative A is incorrect: The optimal risky portfolio is different from the global minimum-variance portfolio. It is the portfolio that provides the best

The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio risk-adjusted return when considering an investor’s preferences for risk and return. Alternative B is incorrect: The global minimum-variance portfolio is not the portfolio with the highest return; portfolios on the efficient frontier that lie above the minimum-variance portfolio offer higher returns. 2.	 Investors with high-risk tolerances would mostly likely choose portfolios that lie: A.	 below the minimum-variance portfolio. B.	 near the upper right of the efficient frontier. C.	 near the lower left portion of the efficient frontier. Solution: The correct response is B. Investors seeking higher returns with a willing­ ness to take on more risk are likely to choose portfolios that lie near the upper right of the efficient frontier (where expected returns and standard deviations are higher). Alternative A is incorrect: Portfolios that lie below the minimum-variance portfolio should not be chosen because they are inefficient, as there are portfolios on the efficient frontier above the minimum-variance portfolio that offer a higher expected return for the same level of risk. Alternative C is incorrect: Investors who want to bear relatively little risk, and therefore expect to earn relatively lower returns, are likely to choose portfolios that lie near the lower left of the efficient frontier (where expected returns and standard deviations are lower). The Minimum-Variance Frontier The minimum-variance frontier comprises a set of portfolios that exhibit the low­ est possible variance, or risk, for a given level of expected return. Finding the minimum-variance frontier adds one additional constraint to the optimization used for the minimum-variance portfolio: the expected return. We aim to minimize port­ folio variance, subject to two constraints: 1.	 a full investment constraint and 2.	 an expected return constraint. Assume again that the portfolio consists of Asset A and Asset B, with weights w A and w B, respectively. The first constraint ensures that the portfolio weights sum to one: w A + w B  =  1. The second constraint determines the expected return of the portfolio: w A r A + w B r B  =  r p. (25) In practice, it is common to include a non-negativity or no-shorting constraint (i.e., w A, w B  ≥  0), but as these are hard to address at an introductory level, we will solve the problem without the non-negativity constraint and then impose it on the solution we obtain. The optimization problem can now be expressed as: Minimize   σ P =  w A σ A + w B σ B + 2 w A w B σ A,B subject to:
The Minimum–Variance Portfolio and the Efficient Frontier w A r A + w B r B  =  r p and w A + w B  =  1, where
r A and r B = the expected returns of Asset A and Asset B, respectively

r p = the target expected return of the portfolio Substituting w B into the expected return constraint gives: w A r A + (1 − w A) r B  =  r p. Solving for w A: w A(r A − r B) + r B  =  r p, w A  = r p − r B _ r A − r B . If w A is to be positive, r P must be at least as large as r B. Similarly: w B  =  1 − w A  = r A − r p _ r A − r B . Next, substitute w A and w B back into the variance formula: σ p 2  =  ( r p − r B _ r A − r B ) σ A + ( r A − r p _ r A − r B ) σ B + 2( r p − r B _ r A − r B )( r A − r p _ r A − r B ) σ A,B. Simplifying this expression, we arrive at: σ p 2  = (r p − r B) 2 σ A + (r A − r p) 2 σ B + 2(r p − r B)(r A − r p) σ A,B

(r A − r B) 2    . (26) Thus, Equation 26 is the equation for the variance of a two-asset portfolio. By varying r p, we can trace out the minimum-variance frontier for the two-asset portfolio: These portfolios are optimal from a risk minimization perspective. The minimum-variance frontier coincides with the efficient frontier when the target portfolio return exceeds the return of the minimum-variance portfolio. In the case of a two-asset portfolio, it is easy to determine the expected return and standard deviation of all points on the efficient frontier. Once we identify the weight, w min,A, associated with the minimum-variance portfolio, we only need to change the constraint, w A  ≥  0 to w A  ≥  w min,A. Covering all possible weights for w A from w min,A to 1 will generate the entire efficient frontier. It is important to distinguish between the minimum‐variance frontier and the efficient frontier, which is its upper segment. Because risk‐averse investors select the highest return at each risk level, they focus on the efficient portion of the frontier rather than on points below it.

In summary, to achieve a target return of 9%, the portfolio manager should allocate 85.1% to the MSCI World Index and 14.9% to the risk-free asset. By combining the MSCI World Index with a risk-free asset, investors can create a range of portfolios, each reflecting a distinct risk–return profile tailored to their preferences. This allocation offers investors flexibility to align portfolio risk with their desired returns. We will continue to explore this allocation in the next lesson. Portfolio Optimization Portfolio optimization seeks to achieve the most efficient allocation of assets by selecting the best possible, or optimal, combination of securities. This optimality can be achieved through the following:

•  Return-constrained optimization by minimizing portfolio risk, σ p, for a given level of return. This method determines the lowest possible risk available at the specified return level, identifying asset combinations that lie on the efficient frontier as well as the inefficient frontier that envelopes the possibility space from the bottom.

•  Risk-constrained optimization by finding the highest expected return E[r p ], for a given level of risk. This approach identifies asset combinations that create portfolios on the efficient frontier, delivering the highest possible return at a specified risk level.
•  Risk-adjusted return optimization by maximizing the Sharpe ratio,

E[r p] − r f _ σ p , where r f represents the risk-free rate. This approach identifies asset combi­ nations that create portfolios with the highest risk-adjusted returns on the efficient frontier. The portfolio optimization process incorporates several key inputs:

•  Expected returns, E[r i], for each individual asset. Return forecasts can be conditioned on the short-term or long-term historical performance of financial assets and asset classes, economic and financial indicators, indus­ try-wide trends, and company-specific factors.

•  Volatility, σ i, for each individual asset. This measure quantifies the dis­ persion of assets’ returns and can be estimated using historical data or forward-looking expectations. Volatility is often measured using the stan­ dard deviation of asset returns.
The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio

•  Asset correlations, ρ i,j, or the off-diagonal covariances from the variance-covariance matrix V. These measures quantify the co-movements between asset returns. Combining assets with correlations strictly less than 1 achieve risk reduction through diversification. The optimization process must also account for investor-specific factors, such as risk tolerance, the capacity and willingness to absorb losses, investment horizon, cash return requirements, and other investment objectives. These considerations significantly influence the optimal portfolio composition, moving away from the optimal combination of assets in the portfolio, and will be addressed throughout the curriculum. The next case study illustrates portfolio optimization with multiple assets and shows how combining equities, emerging markets, and government bonds can generate efficient portfolios.

explain the selection of an optimal portfolio, given an investor’s risk aversion and the capital allocation line, and how this extends to the market portfolio and the capital market line An optimal investment portfolio balances risk and return and reflects an investor’s preferences. This lesson explores the theoretical foundations of achieving that balance and selecting an optimal portfolio. While there are many versions of portfolio theory that span a range of assumptions, the theory we explore in this lesson relies on several key assumptions that simplify complex relationships and facilitate the construction, analysis, and implementation of theoretical models:

•  Investors are rational and risk-averse. All investors are assumed to be ratio­ nal and risk-averse; they make decisions aimed at maximizing their utility or satisfaction. They prefer higher return investments to lower return invest­ ments and lower risk investments to higher risk investments.  Investors will choose investments that offer the best risk–return trade-off according to their personal preferences.
Optimal Portfolio Selection

•  Investors have a single period time horizon. All investors are assumed to have the same one-period time horizon. They make investment decisions at the beginning of the period and evaluate their results at the end of the period. This single-period horizon—which could be one year, one month, or any other duration—simplifies calculations and evaluations of risk and return, as well as portfolio optimization.

•  Investors pay no taxes or transaction costs. All investors are assumed to trade securities without incurring taxes or transaction costs. This assump­ tion simplifies the analysis by focusing solely on investment performance and market behavior.

•  There is a risk-free asset that can be bought or sold. A risk-free asset, such as a short-term government bill with no default risk, is assumed to exist, which investors can borrow and lend at a constant risk-free rate without constraint and with no repo charge on a short position. This risk-free asset provides a guaranteed return with no risk, offering a baseline for evaluating and com­ paring other investments and allowing for the comparative evaluation of the performance of riskier assets. While there are more advanced versions of the theory, in which other portfolios play the role of the risk-free asset, we do not consider them in this learning module. These assumptions are incorporated in models that are implemented daily in both investment-management processes and portfolio-construction decisions. First, we discuss investor risk preferences and utility functions. Then augmenting these assumptions with some additional assumptions, we derive key concepts, such as the capital allocation line (CAL), the capital market line (CML), and the capital asset pricing model (CAPM). The estimation and use of the CAPM to model risk and expected returns for assets and portfolios is discussed throughout the CFA® Program curriculum. Investor Risk Preferences and Utility Functions Risk preference refers to individuals’ or investors’ attitudes towards risk when making investment decisions and determines how much risk, uncertainty, or variability in returns they are willing to assume in exchange for potential gains. We typically divide risk preferences into three categories:

•  Risk-seeking investors prefer gambles with uncertain outcomes over guar­ anteed outcomes with the same expected value because they derive extra utility from the uncertainty. They may even accept a lower expected return, such as a gamble with an expected value of CNY45 over a guaranteed CNY50 due to their preference for risk. This tendency is evident in behav­ iors like buying lottery tickets or gambling in casinos, where the expected returns are usually negative.

•  Risk-neutral investors are indifferent between gambles and guaranteed out­ comes with the same expected value. These investors focus solely on returns and are indifferent to the level of risk when making investment decisions. Consequently, they prefer higher expected return investments, regardless of the associated risk. This attitude is more common when the investment represents a small fraction of their total wealth, such as a billionaire being indifferent between a gamble or a CNY50 guaranteed return.
The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio

•  Risk-averse investors prefer less variable (or even guaranteed) outcomes over gambles, even if the gamble has a higher expected value. They aim to minimize risk for a given return or maximize return for a given level of risk. For example, they may prefer a guaranteed payoff of CNY45 over a gamble with an expected value of CNY50. Real world investors, with few exceptions, are generally risk averse. But for the development of asset pricing, asset allocation, and portfolio management models, the assumptions of risk neutrality can offer theoretical insights. Specifically, we consider people or institutions to be risk neutral when they engage in many independent trades or bets. By the Law of Large Numbers, the variance of those trades averages out, making the expected return almost certain over time. For instance, institutional investors implement many small trades in liquid markets. Because they’re involved in so many trades, the risk attributable to a single trade becomes negligible over time. The assumption that these large institutional investors act as if they are risk neutral is important for understanding concepts like arbitrage: These investors stabilize returns across different markets by constantly engaging in small transactions with limited variability and, on aggregate, achieve nearly certain outcomes. Understanding risk preferences is important in developing an investment strategy and creating asset portfolios that balance risk and returns. A simple implementation of utility theory allows us to quantify the rankings of investment choices using risk and return. Utility functions The utility function in finance represents an investor’s preferences, incorporating both an investment’s expected return and associated risk. The following utility func­ tion is widely utilized in portfolio theory for its simplicity and the clear implications it offers for risk aversion: U  =  E[r] −  1 _ A σ 2, (27) where
E[r] = the expected return
σ 2 = the variance of the portfolio as a measure of risk

A = the coefficient of risk aversion An investor’s utility increases with expected return but decreases with risk and the investor’s coefficient of risk aversion, suggesting that investors experience dimin­ ishing marginal utility as risk increases. As we shall later see, the coefficient of risk aversion is seldomly less than 1 and has repeatedly been documented to lie between 2 and 3. Other functions, such as a logarithmic utility function and a power-law utility function, are also used in practice. An example of a commonly used utility is the mean–variance utility that rep­ resents an investor’s preferences using only two factors: the expected return (mean) and the risk (variance) of an investment, or: U p  =  U(E[r P], σ P), (28) where
U(⋅) = the utility function
E[r p] = the expected return of the investment
σ P = the standard deviation of the investment returns You will note that Equation 27 is a special case of Equation 28.

Optimal Portfolio Selection This definition of utility contrasts with the classical economists’ definition of utility, which depends on the level of, and changes in, an investor’s wealth. Exhibit 22 summarizes differences in risk preferences and risk aversion. Closely related to an investor’s risk preference is their risk tolerance, the degree of risk an investor is willing to accept to achieve their investment goals. Risk tolerance is inversely related to risk aversion: A higher risk tolerance implies greater willingness to take risks and lower aversion to risk. Exhibit 22: Risk Preference and Risk Aversion Risk Preference Behavior Risk-Aversion Coefficient Utility Function Investment Preference Risk-seeking Additional utility from increased risk A  <  0 Higher return and higher risk at any given level of return Risk-neutral Indifferent to the level of risk A  =  0 U  =  E[r] Focuses solely on expected return; indiffer­ ent to the level of risk Risk-averse Inclined to avoid risk A  >  0 U  =  E[r] −  1 _ A σ 2 Higher return and lower risk at any given level of return Risk tolerance is not fixed; it tends to change with age, health, wealth, and family circumstances, as well as with the economic environment. There is considerable variation in the average and socially acceptable level of risk tolerance across countries and cultures. We distinguish between absolute, relative, and varying risk aversion:
•  Absolute risk aversion measures how much an investor’s utility changes with each incremental increase in risk, holding wealth constant.
•  Relative risk aversion measures the proportion of wealth an investor is pre­ pared to risk, highlighting how risk aversion adapts in response to changes in wealth.

•  Varying levels of risk aversion: As an investor’s wealth changes, the aver­ sion to risk changes. Indifference curves An indifference curve graphically represents different risk–return combinations that provide the same level of utility. Each point on an indifference curve represents a unique risk and return combination, but all points on the same indifference curve provide the same utility. Exhibit 23 shows indifference curves for different investor types.

The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio Exhibit 23: Indifference Curves for Different Investor Types 9.0 0.0 0.2 0.4 Risk (Standard Deviation ) Convex (Risk-Seeking) Concave (Risk-Averse) 0.6 0.8 1.0 9.5 Expected Return E[r] 10.5 10.0 11.0 Indifference Curves for Risk-Seeking, Risk-Neutral, and Risk-Averse Investors Utility Function: U = E[r] – A2 Utility Levels and Risk Aversion Coefficients Risk-Seeking A = –2, U = 10 Risk-Seeking A = –1.25, U = 10 Risk-Seeking A = –1.5, U = 10 Risk-Neutral A = 0, U = 10 Risk-Averse A = 2.5, U = 10 Risk-Averse A = 2.75, U = 10 Risk-Averse A = 2, U = 10 The slope of an indifference curve represents the marginal rate of substitution between risk and return (i.e., the rate at which an investor is willing to exchange additional risk for additional return while maintaining the same level of utility). A steeper pos­ itive slope indicates greater risk aversion, as the investor demands a higher return to compensate for increased risk.

•  Risk-averse investors have concave utility functions in wealth, which trans­ lates to convex indifference curves, indicating diminishing marginal utility of return (or wealth). As risk increases, increasingly higher returns are needed to maintain the same utility level.

•  Risk-seeking investors have convex utility functions in wealth, which trans­ lates to concave indifference curves, indicating increasing marginal utility of return (or wealth). As risk increases, progressively smaller returns are needed to sustain the same utility level.

The utility of the three investments, assuming a risk aversion coefficient of A  =  4, is calculated as: Investment A: U A  =  0.12 −  1 _ × 4 × (0.30) 2  =  0.12 − 2 × 0.09  =  0.12 − 0.18  =  − 0.06. The utility of the three investments, assuming a risk-aversion coefficient of A  =  2, is calculated as: Investment A: U A  =  0.12 −  1 _ × 2 × (0.30) 2  =  0.12 − 1 × 0.09  =  0.12 − 0.09  =  0.03. The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio C.	 Investment C Solution: The correct response is C. The utility of the three investments, assuming a risk-aversion coefficient of A  =  − 4, is calculated as: Investment A: U A  =  0.12 −  1 _ × (− 4) × (0.30) 2  =  0.12 − (− 2) × 0.09  =  0.12 + 0.18  =  0.30. Investment B: U B  =  0.15 −  1 _ × (− 4) × (0.35) 2  =  0.15 − (− 2) × 0.1225  =  0.15 + 0.245 =  0.395. Investment C: U C  =  0.21 −  1 _ × (− 4) × (0.40) 2  =  0.21 − (− 2) × 0.16  =  0.21 + 0.32  =  0.53. A risk-seeking investor with a risk-aversion coefficient of −4 should choose Investment C because it yields the highest utility. Observe that the utility function increases, both on account of the expected return and the variance. The next section illustrates how utility and risk preferences influence portfolio selection. The Capital Allocation Line (CAL) When a risk-free asset is available, investors can combine a risk-free asset with a risky portfolio, P. Such combinations expand the opportunity set beyond just the curved efficient frontier of risky assets under the following additional assumptions:
•  The risk-free asset has a standard deviation of 0.
•  The standard deviation and the expected return of Q are each strictly greater than the risk-free rate.
•  Investors have access to only these two assets.

•  Investors can freely borrow and lend money at the same constant risk-free rate. Combining a risk-free asset with a risky portfolio allows investors to create a combination that earns the following expected return: E[r p]  =  w f × r f + (1 − w f) × E[r Q], (29) where w f is the proportion invested in the risk-free asset and E[r Q] is the expected return of the risky portfolio. As the risk-free asset has zero standard deviation, only the risky portfolio influences the overall standard deviation: σ p  =  (1 − w f) × σ Q, (30) whereσ r is the standard deviation of the risky portfolio. Then, a combination of the risk-free rate, the expected return, and the standard deviation of the risky portfolio gives the following: E[r p]  =  r f + E[r Q] − r f _ σ Q  σ p. (31)

Optimal Portfolio Selection The straight line from the risk-free rate (on the vertical axis) to a tangential portfolio on the efficient frontier of risk assets is the optimal capital allocation line, often referred to as just the capital allocation line (CAL as shown in Exhibit 24). Equation 31 identifies all the combinations of risk and return that can be realized by combining a risk-free asset and the risky portfolio, P. The expected return of this portfolio, E[r p], increases linearly with its standard deviation, σ p, which in turn increases as the fraction of the portfolio invested in the risky portfolio increases. Exhibit 24 shows the highest attainable utility curve that is tangent to the efficient frontier. This point of tangency offers the optimal risk–return trade-off: It maximizes the investor’s utility given their risk preferences. Exhibit 24: Capital Allocation Line, Indifference Curves, and the Market Portfolio Less Risk-Averse More Risk-Averse Capital Allocation Line Market Portfolio Risk/Standard Deviation Expected Return Risk-Free Asset Risk aversion impacts portfolio choice for individuals. To maximize utility, an inves­ tor should choose a portfolio that lies at the point of tangency between their highest attainable indifference curve and the CAL. Consequently:
•  Risk-averse investors allocate more to the risk-free asset, moving left on the CAL toward lower risk and return.

•  Risk-tolerant investors allocate more to the risky portfolio, moving right on the CAL toward higher risk and return, potentially using leverage to boost returns. The slope of the CAL, E[r P] − r f _ σ P , captures the trade-off between risk and return of a portfolio. It is the Sharpe ratio, a common measure of the risk-adjusted return. Steeper slopes indicate higher Sharpe ratios and more desirable risk–return profiles, and they imply a higher excess return per unit of risk.
The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio
Example 15

Calculating the Sharpe Ratio We previously calculated the weights of portfolios that combine the risky port­ folio, proxied by the MSCI World Index, and a risk-free asset. The weights were adjusted to achieve target returns of 9% and 12%, respectively. The resulting portfolio compositions and their risk characteristics are as follows:
Portfolio Target Return Weight of MSCI World Index Standard Deviation A 9% 85.1% 12.59% B 12% 117.1% 17.32%

Compute the Sharpe ratio for each portfolio assuming a risk-free rate of 1%. The Sharpe ratio for Portfolio A is calculated as: Sharpe ratio A  = r A − r f _ σ A   =   9% − 1% _ 12.59%   ≈  0.635. Similarly, for Portfolio B: Sharpe ratio B  = r B − r f _ σ B   =   12% − 1% _ 17.32%   ≈  0.635. Both portfolios have the same Sharpe ratio because they are on the same CAL. The Sharpe ratio is the slope of the CAL, so all combinations of the MSCI World Index and the risk-free asset have the same Sharpe ratio. Portfolio B uses leverage: Its MSCI World Index weight is 117.1%, and it borrows at the risk-free rate to achieve its higher target return. Combining the risk-free asset with a non-efficient risky portfolio would result in a CAL that lies below the efficient frontier, a suboptimal portfolio combination. In the next section, we will explore the capital market line, a special case of the CAL. The Capital Market Line (CML) The capital market line (CML) is a special case of the capital allocation line (CAL). Instead of the risky portfolio, the risk-free asset is combined with the market portfolio that includes all available risky assets weighted by their market values; it is mean– variance efficient, meaning it has the highest Sharpe ratio of all possible portfolios. Consequently, CML is drawn from the risk-free asset to this market portfolio and represents the set of mean–variance efficient, or optimal, portfolios. This result is closely tied to the mutual fund theorem, which states that all investors can achieve efficient portfolios by combining only two assets: the market portfolio and the risk-free asset. Investors adjust their risk by borrowing or lending at the risk-free rate while holding the market portfolio. In practice, defining the true market portfolio poses challenges, since it should theoretically encompass all investable assets, including stocks, bonds, real estate, commodities, and more. In practice, we rely on broad stock market indexes (e.g., MSCI World Index, FTSE 100, or Hang Seng) as proxies. This limitation affects the practical application. Mathematically, the CML is formulated as: E[r]  =  r f + E[r m] − r f _ σ m  σ p, (32) whereE[r m] is the expected return on the market portfolio andσ m is the standard deviation of the market portfolio.

Optimal Portfolio Selection Along the CML, the ratio of the standard deviation of an asset or a portfolio, σ p, to the standard deviation of the market portfolio, σ m, indicates how sensitive the portfolio’s returns are to the returns of the market portfolio. This ratio is closely related to the concept of beta (symbol β), which more precisely incorporates the correlation between the asset (or portfolio) and the market and is typically defined as β  =  ρ p,m × σ p _ σ m , where ρ p,m is the correlation between the portfolio’s returns and the market’s returns. We will discuss beta in more detail in the next section. Exhibit 25 illustrates the CML that originates from the risk-free rate on the ver­ tical axis (y-axis) and passes through the market portfolio, which lies on the efficient frontier above a cloud of points that represent the many individual securities within the market portfolio. Exhibit 25: Efficient Frontier and Capital Market Line Risk-Free Rate Rf = 3.00% 2.5 5.0 7.5 10.0 12.5 15.0 17.5 20.0 0.6 0.5 0.4 0.7 0.8 0.9 Markowitz Efficient Frontier and Capital Market Line (CML) Expected Return, E[r] (%) Sharpe Ratio 0.0 0.00 0.02 0.04 0.06 0.08 0.10 0.12 0.14 0.16 Risk, σ Market Portfolio: E[r] = 11.99%, σ = 0.10 Capital Market Line (CML): E[rp] = rf + σp with Slope of 0.93, E[rm] – rf σm The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) is a simple model of market equilibrium. As the market portfolio lies on the efficient frontier, the expected return of any security or portfolio is determined solely by its beta, β, the systematic and non-diversifiable market risk. CAPM further assumes the following:
•  All investors hold the same views on the risk and return of individual securities and hold mean–variance optimal portfolios that reflect their risk tolerance.
The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio
•  All investors invest in portfolios that lie on the mean–variance efficient frontier, but each with their own level of risk aversion.
•  The market is in equilibrium, meaning that supply and demand for securi­ ties are balanced so that all securities are owned by someone.

•  All investors are price takers, accept market prices as given, and cannot influence them individually. Systematic risk, beta, β A security’s systematic risk, the risk that cannot be diversified away, is measured by β, and formally, beta is expressed as: β i  = σ i,m _ σ m 2    = ρ i,m × σ i  × σ m _ σ m 2     = ρ i,m × σ i _ σ m , (33) where
σ i,m = the covariance between the returns of asset i and the return on the market portfolio
σ m 2  = the variance of the market portfolio’s returns
ρ i,m = the correlation coefficient between the returns of asset i and the market returns
σ i = the standard deviation of the returns of asset i
σ m = the standard deviation of the market returns As beta reflects the sensitivity to market risk, σ m, it determines returns relative to the risk in the market:
•  When β i  >  1, the expected return of the security is higher than that of the market.

•  When β i  <  1, its expected return is lower than that of the market. Only systematic (market) risk affects expected returns because investors can elim­ inate non-systematic (security-specific) risk through diversification. Non-systematic risk does not influence expected returns. Security market line The security market line (SML) expresses that the expected return of an individual security, i, is determined as: E[r i]  =  r f + E[r m] − r f _ σ m 2   σ i,m, (34) where σ i,m is the covariance of security i with the market portfolio and σ m 2  is the variance of the market portfolio. In the special case when the SML is applied to the market portfolio, β m  = σ m,m _ σ m 2    =  1, and then the expected return derived from the SML is identical to that obtained from the CML. CAPM and its estimation In compact form, CAPM is: E[r i]  =  r f + β i(E[r m] − r f), (35)
Optimal Portfolio Selection where β i is the beta value of asset i and is equal to σ p / σ m.
Example 16

Suppose the risk-free rate, r f, is 3%, the expected market return, E[r m], is 8%, and the beta value, β i, of an asset is 1.2. The expected return, E[r i], of the asset can be calculated as follows: E[r i]  =  0.03 + 1.2 × (0.08 − 0.03)  =  0.03 + 1.2 × 0.05  =  0.03 + 0.06  =  0.09 =  9%. Thus, according to the CAPM, the expected return of the asset is 9%. The market risk premium, E[r m] − r f, represents the additional return over and above the risk-free rate that can be expected—but not guaranteed—to be earned by holding the risky market portfolio instead of the risk-free asset. As β measures the systematic risk of each individual asset relative to the market, it links the risk premium of an asset with that of the market.

In practice, both the expected return of the market and β i must be estimated from data, as they are unobservable. An asset beta is most commonly estimated using linear regression, which we cover later in the curriculum. Historical returns for the asset and the market index, typically weekly or monthly returns, are collected over a period of one to five years. The asset’s excess returns, r i − r f, are then regressed against the market’s excess returns, r m − r f. The regression equation takes the form: r i − r f  =  α + β i(r m − r f) + ϵ i, (36) where
α = the intercept

ϵ = the error term. The slope coefficient, β i, from this regression is an estimate of the asset’s histor­ ical beta value, which measures its sensitivity to market movements over the period covered by the regression. Once β i is estimated, it can be used in the following CAPM formula, Equation 37, to estimate the expected return of the asset: E[r i]  =  r f + β i(E[r m] − r f), (37) where
E[r i] = the expected return of the asset

E[r m] = the expected market return. The choice of time period—whether daily, weekly, or monthly returns are used—for the regression affects the beta estimate. Longer periods provide more stable estimates, but they may not reflect recent changes in the asset’s risk profile. The choice of market index to proxy for the theoretical market portfolio impacts results as well. Common choices include broad market indices, such as the S&P 500 for the United States, FTSE 100 for the United Kingdom (London), and the CAC 40 for France (Paris). The CAPM assumes a linear relationship between risk and return, a relation that may not always hold. Additionally, CAPM theoretically predicts that if markets are efficient, α (alpha) should be zero. However, empirical research often finds non-zero alpha values, which has led to critiques of the model.

Optimal portfolio selection balances risk with return in line with the investor’s risk preferences. Starting with assumptions about risk aversion, single-period horizons, and the existence of a risk-free asset, we have discussed three key ideas:
•  CAL shows what risk and return combinations can be achieved by combin­ ing a risk-free asset and a chosen risky portfolio.
•  CML is a special case where the chosen risky portfolio is the market portfolio.

•  CAPM links expected return to its systematic (market) risk via beta. The curriculum will revisit the ideas of mean–variance optimization, risk–return trade-offs, and systematic versus idiosyncratic risk throughout as they remain the cornerstones of modern portfolio theory and investment practice. Limitations Both in practice and reality, several assumptions underpinning traditional portfolio-management theories may not hold true:
•  The widely used assumption that financial asset returns follow a normal distribution is not supported by empirical evidence: Asset returns exhibit significant skewness and kurtosis.
Optimal Portfolio Selection
•  The assumption of constant correlations between asset returns is problem­ atic as correlations change over time, especially during periods of market stress.
•  Real-world financial markets are not perfectly efficient and reflect informa­ tion asymmetries that can lead to the mispricing of assets.

•  Estimation errors, even small measurement errors or inaccuracies in estimating expected returns and volatility, can have a significant impact on expected return, risk, and correlation calculations. Such errors can meaningfully impact the assets held, as well as their weights, in the optimal portfolio.

•  Historical returns, variances, and correlations may only reflect a historical relationship that no longer exists because of changing market expectations, valuations, or material changes to the assets. Practical constraints also play a crucial role in real-world portfolio management:
•  Transaction costs, if ignored, can lead to unrealistic portfolio rebalancing strategies.

•  Taxes affect investment performance in two main ways: returns arise from periodic capital distributions and capital appreciation. Each return can face different, sometimes punitive, tax rates, so the after-tax return is neces­ sarily lower than the pre-tax return. The net impact of taxes can signifi­ cantly affect after-tax net returns and alter the composition of the optimal portfolio.

•  Finally, opportunistically realizing capital losses to reduce capital gains and capital-gains taxes may change realized after-tax portfolio returns and risk-adjusted returns. Although taxes can have an outsized impact on the performance of a portfolio, we do not address tax-optimized portfolio construction, as it is a complex topic. Taxes depend not only on distributions (gains and losses) on a particular portfolio but also gains and losses on other portfolios held by the investor.

1.	 The line depicting the total risk and expected return of portfolio combinations of a risk-free asset and any risky asset is the: A.	 capital market line. B.	 security market line. C.	 capital allocation line. Solution: The correct response is C. A capital allocation line (CAL) plots the expected return and total risk of combinations of the risk-free asset and a risky asset (or a portfolio of risky assets). It illustrates the risk–return trade-off for these combinations and shows how different allocations between the riskfree asset and the risky portfolio impact the portfolio’s expected return and risk. Alternative A is incorrect: The capital market line (CML) is a special case of the CAL and represents the risk–return trade-off for efficient portfolios that include the market portfolio (a portfolio of all market capitalization-weight­ ed risky assets) and a risk-free asset, but it is specific to the market portfolio and not just any risky portfolio.

sections.title: Summary: The Return And Risk Of A Financial Portfolio

blocks.x: •  Portfolio statistics, such as returns, variances, and covariances, are funda­ mental to effective portfolio management and investment strategy.
•  A portfolio that holds 30 or more well-diversified assets can capture most of the benefits of diversification.
•  Portfolio optimization involves finding the optimal mix of assets under certain constraints.
•  The minimum-variance portfolio offers the lowest variance among all feasi­ ble portfolios and is the lowest point of the efficient frontier.

•  The efficient frontier consists of the set of optimal portfolios that maximize the expected return for each level of risk. The efficient frontier lies on the upper boundary of the set of feasible portfolios.
•  Investors’ attitudes toward risk can be broadly categorized as risk-averse, risk-neutral, or risk-seeking, and are characterized by the coefficient of risk aversion.
•  The capital allocation line (CAL) depicts the trade-offs between risk and return that can be achieved by combining a risk-free asset with a risky portfolio.

•  The capital market line (CML) is a special case of the capital allocation line and represents the trade-offs between risk and return that can be achieved by combining a risk-free asset with the market portfolio.
•  The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) implies that the expected return of an asset depends solely on its systematic risk, measured by its market risk.

•  Limitations of traditional portfolio management theories include their assumptions of normally distributed returns, stable and predictable vari­ ances and covariances, and practical constraints, such as transaction costs and taxes.

sections.title: Introduction: Simulation Of Financial Asset Prices And Returns

blocks.x: This learning module introduces simulation methodologies commonly used in finance. Simulations begin with assumptions about the distributions of variables at one or multiple points in time and allow us to assess their impact on a target function. These techniques are highly useful in evaluating risk and returns, portfolio optimization, and cash flow and liquidity modeling. We begin with historical simulation, where scenarios are drawn directly from historical data instead of being simulated. Then, we cover bootstrap simulation, or bootstrapping, which generates scenarios from an empirical distribution based on historical data. We conclude with Monte Carlo simulation, which generates multiple random scenarios based on distributional assumptions. These methods provide powerful tools for analyzing uncertainty and making informed financial decisions. These methods form an integral part of financial decision making, including scenario analysis, asset valuation, portfolio management, return attribution, and risk management. blocks.x: RETURNS 1.	 Monte Carlo simulation is most appropriate for valuation analysis when the investment has: A.	 a final payoff that is path dependent. B.	 significant volatility observed in the underlying security. C.	 a contingent claim that is tied to a stochastic yield curve. Solution: The correct response is A. Path dependency in a contingent claim implies that the valuation cannot simply consider the probability-weighted expec­ tations of the final values influencing the final payout. Rather, intermediate values throughout the life of the asset are crucial. Such situations do not easily lend themselves to formulaic solutions, and Monte Carlo simulation is ideal to model such assets. B is incorrect: Significant observed volatility has an impact on any valuation approach. C is incorrect: Yield curve contingent claims, such as simple swaps, do not necessarily require simulation to analyze pricing. 2.	 Which of the following assumptions is implicit in historical simulation? A.	 The expected mean price change for most financial assets is zero. B.	 Past price changes form a reasonable proxy for future price changes. C.	 Potential price changes can be modeled with a multivariate normal distribution. Solution: The correct response is B. In historical simulation, past price changes are applied to current exposures to model the potential distribution of out­ comes. The implicit assumption is that potential future price changes will distribute as they did in the observation period. A is incorrect: An assumption of an expected mean price change of zero for most financial assets is a common assumption made in risk analyses. C is incorrect: The assumption that potential price changes can be modeled with a multivariate normal distribution is a common assumption in Monte Carlo simulation. 3. describe historical simulation and explain how it can be used in investment applications Overview of Simulation Methods Simulation is a method used to predict potential outcomes for a system or calcula­ tion based on theoretical scenarios. The simulation process involves defining a clear objective, selecting specific variables for simulation, assigning values to those variables, analyzing the resulting scenarios, and then compiling and interpreting the outcomes. The key steps of the simulation process are outlined in Exhibit 1. Exhibit 1: Steps in the Simulation Process Setup/Parameterize Scenario Generation Scenario Evaluation/Calculation Engine Result Compilation/ Analysis
Historical Simulation The specific steps in a simulation are as follows:

•  Step 1: Setup/parameterize. The first step in a simulation is to clearly define the goal, specifying the output variables to be simulated, such as a price, a return, or a value. Once the output variables are identified and the appropri­ ate input variables are selected, the calculations required to connect these inputs to the desired outputs for each scenario are determined. One typical goal is to evaluate portfolio risk-adjusted performance over a one-year horizon. In this case, the key output variable is the risk-adjusted return. Input variables include historical stock price data and changes in the interest rate spread, with their statistical properties (mean, variance, correlations).

•  Step 2: Scenario generation. The second step generates the scenarios. These scenarios can range from simple, user-defined input information to com­ plex, machine-generated sets of input vectors, with each set representing a different scenario. Simulation models often generate thousands of simula­ tions, if not more!

•  Step 3: Scenario evaluation/calculation engine. In the third step, the gen­ erated scenarios are processed by a calculation engine, which applies the defined calculations from the setup/parameterize phase to each input sce­ nario, producing the corresponding output values or vectors. If we were aiming to analyze the expected risk/return trade off, the substeps here might involve the following: a.	 Calculate individual asset returns. b.	 Calculate portfolio returns based on asset weights. c.	 Calculate risk metrics and risk-adjusted performance measures.

•  Step 4: Result compilation/analysis. The final step collects the outputs from the calculation engine and then analyzes these results to infer conclusions about the output variables, thereby addressing the objectives outlined in the setup/parameterize phase. For a risk/reward analysis objective, the final phase would aggregate results across all scenarios to construct a probability distribution of risk-adjusted returns, which allows the portfolio manager to quantify potential downside risks, assess the portfolio’s risk-adjusted performance, and optimize asset allocation strategies. The implementation of the different simulation approaches follows a similar pro­ cess. Three simulation approaches are commonly used:

•  Historical simulation estimates the behavior of a system by using actual historical data to model future scenarios. Rather than generating random inputs, it relies on observed market conditions or other real-world data to assess the potential outcomes. This approach helps analyze how a system might behave under previously experienced conditions, providing a clear picture of potential risks based on historical events.

•  Bootstrap simulation resamples historical data with replacement to create new synthetic datasets. Unlike historical simulation, which directly uses past data, bootstrap simulation introduces randomness by allowing repeated sampling of the same data points. This preserves the empirical distribution

Simulation of Financial Asset Prices and Returns of the original data while accounting for variability and reducing the risk of overfitting to specific historical events, offering a more flexible approach to scenario generation.

•  Monte Carlo simulation is a computational technique that uses random sampling to estimate the behavior or outcome of a system. It requires distri­ butional assumptions on a set of input variables. The primary difference among the three approaches lies in how they source their scenarios. A well-structured simulation system can accommodate scenarios from any source, including the three approaches discussed in this learning module. A robust simulation framework should include a central engine that can process a sufficiently large number of scenarios to deliver precise estimates. Exhibit 2 compares the three simulation approaches across the key steps outlined in Exhibit 1. Exhibit 2: Comparing the Steps for Different Simulation Approaches Simulation Approach Step 1: Setup/ Parameterize Step 2: Scenario Generation Step 3: Scenario Evaluation Step 4: Result Analysis Historical Simulation Use historical data to ini­ tialize model parameters. Incorporate actual past observations for scenario inputs. Run the model using each his­ torical scenario. Examine perfor­ mance under real-world conditions encountered in the past. Bootstrap Simulation Adopt historical data to define parameters (with replacement). Formulate syn­ thetic scenarios by resampling the observed dataset. Conduct cal­ culations for each resampled scenario. Assess vari­ ability while preserving the original data structure. Monte Carlo Simulation Specify probabil­ ity distributions for model inputs. Draw random samples from these distribu­ tions to shape scenario inputs. Execute calcula­ tions using each random input vector. Evaluate the resulting distribution of outputs to determine risks and probabilities. The three simulation approaches create the most differentiation in Step 2: the actual development of the scenarios. Otherwise, there is little difference in the other steps in the simulation process. Historical Simulation Overview Historical simulation models potential outcomes using historical data. In finance, simulations use historical asset prices and returns to capture real-world market behaviors without imposing distributional assumptions. It offers the benefit of being easy to both explain and build narratives around. It allows for such statements as “the portfolio would gain INR300 million if we have the same market movements as those that occurred on July 16 last year.” Historical simulation directly applies past market movements to current factors under the implicit assumption that historical price changes provide a reasonable approximation of future price movements and risks. This method avoids making

Historical Simulation assumptions about the underlying distributions of asset returns, capturing real-world patterns such as fat tails or high excess kurtosis (leptokurtic distributions). Effectively, historical simulation assumes that past data represent the full population Similarly, historical simulation can capture volatility clustering, where periods of high volatility tend to be followed by more high volatility and periods of low volatility are followed by more low volatility. However, the assumption that future market conditions will resemble past ones may not always be true, particularly during unprecedented events or regime shifts. Implementing Historical Simulation A simulation engine can be designed to accept scenarios from multiple input sources. In historical simulation, this involves assembling a set of scenarios based on actual historical market movements. For each input variable and each historical data point, we assign the corresponding historical change to that variable, as illustrated in Exhibit 3. Exhibit 3: Simulation Framework Applied to Historical Simulation Setup/Parameterize Scenario Generation Scenario Evaluation/ Calculation Engine Result Compilation/ Analysis Select Valuation/ Risk Factors Select Historical Dates For the Historical Dates and Factors, Determine Scenarios To construct a robust simulation, key valuation and risk factors need to be identified, which serve as the fundamental inputs in the simulation process. For equities, the primary variables are usually continuously compounded (logarithmic) price returns: r t  =  ln( P t _ P t−1 ). For fixed-income instruments, the simulation models changes in the yield curve. The price of a bond is determined by discounting future cash flows using simulated yields: PV B  =  ∑ t=1 T CF t _ (1 + y t) t . Historical simulation can be used to calculate value at risk (VaR) by applying historical returns to current portfolio positions. This method captures real-world market behav­ iors without relying on assumptions about the distribution of returns. The following case study explains how historical simulation can be used to compute the profit and loss distribution of a simple long-only portfolio, an investment strategy where the portfolio holds purchased assets with the expectation that their value will appreciate over a prolonged period time and there is no shorting of securities.

Features of Historical Simulation Historical simulation is a valuable tool for financial analysis, but its implementation often requires attention. Controlling for potentially missing data, unreliable data, or data integrity is crucial when conducting historical simulation because unreliable data can undermine the accuracy of the results. In the context of global investment portfolios, missing data may be caused by the following:

•  Asynchronous global markets. Different markets operate on their own holiday schedules, leading to non-trading days that are not globally synchro­ nized. Unplanned market closures can also happen due to extraordinary events, such as technology outages, required halts to trading, or natural disasters.
Historical Simulation

•  Non-existence of securities during the simulation period. Some securities may not have existed throughout the historical window under consideration. For example, an equity that was listed after the simulation period lacks his­ torical price data.

•  Thinly traded securities. Instruments with low trading volumes may have sparse or unreliable pricing data, making accurate modeling challenging. To address this issue, it is essential to approach the simulation process with an eye to compensate for potential deficiencies. One common approach is to use a proxy, a substitute financial instrument used to represent another security that lacks sufficient historical data for analysis. It approximates the behavior of the original security. A proxy might be created by taking a weighted average of similar financial instruments whose historical data are available. A proxy can compensate for missing data in the simulation process, ensuring that the analysis remains accurate and aligns with its objectives. Applying historical price changes directly to fixed-income instruments can lead to misleading conclusions. The appropriate methodology for fixed-income instruments involves focusing on changes in benchmark yields or prices and not the prices of the actual bond. For instance, consider an Australian investor conducting a historical simulation using the past year’s data for an Australian government bond that matures tomorrow, in one day. Despite the bond’s negligible market risk due to its imminent maturity, using last year’s price changes may incorrectly suggest significant volatility. It is preferable to examine the yield changes for a set of benchmark maturities, such as the one-month, six-month, one-year, or two-year maturities, and then infer the corresponding yield changes for the bond in question. Alternatively, we could analyze the implied price changes for zero-coupon bonds at these benchmark maturities and evaluate how those changes would impact the bond’s cash flows. We end this section by listing the strengths and weaknesses of historical simulation. The strengths of historical simulation include the following:

•  Simplicity. Historical simulation does not rely on complex modeling assumptions or distributions. It simply applies historical market conditions to current portfolios, making it straightforward to implement. Yet, despite the simplicity, historical simulation is widely used to analyze complex securities.
•  No assumptions on distributions. Since it uses historical data, historical simulation eliminates the need to make assumptions about the distribution of returns.
•  Real-world data. By using real historical data, historical simulation provides a realistic view of how a portfolio may behave under previously observed market conditions, including extreme events.
•  No correlation modeling. Because historical simulation uses actual market data, the correlations between assets are inherently preserved, requiring no additional correlation modeling.

•  Low computational cost. Historical simulation is less computationally demanding because it does not require the generation of new data or scenarios. The following are some disadvantages and weaknesses of using historical simulation:

•  Backward looking. Historical simulation is entirely based on past market conditions, which may not accurately predict future events, especially in the case of unprecedented market shocks or structural changes.
Simulation of Financial Asset Prices and Returns

•  Limited scenario variety. The simulation is constrained by the available his­ torical data and more specifically the historical data actually selected, which may not include extreme or uncommon scenarios that could occur in the future.

•  Data limitations. The quality and scope of historical simulation depend on the availability and completeness of historical market data. If the dataset is limited, so is the robustness of the simulation results.

describe bootstrap resampling, and explain how it can be used in investment applications Bootstrapping Overview Resampling is a computational technique that repeatedly draws samples from observed data to make inferences about population parameters. It offers an alternative to tradi­ tional parametric approaches and is particularly useful when distributional assumptions are uncertain or sample sizes are small. Bootstrapping, one of the most widely used resampling methods, uses computer simulations to estimate statistical distributions. It generates these distributions by resampling with replacement from the observed data, treating the sample as a proxy for the population. As samples are taken from the data, they can be analyzed and we can arrive at a result for each sample, which allows bootstrapping to approximate the sampling distribution of a target statistic without requiring explicit assumptions about the underlying population. Resampling with replacement means that after each data point is randomly selected, it is returned to the dataset before the next selection, allowing the same item to be chosen multiple times. Each data point has a selection probability of  1 _ n  in each draw, where n is the sample size. For example, given a sample [2, 5, 8], one possible resample with replacement could be [5, 5, 8], where the value 5 is selected twice. Another res­ ample could be [2, 2, 5], where 2 is selected twice. This ability to generate multiple resamples enables bootstrapping to simulate a sampling distribution, even with a small original dataset. Bootstrapping differs from historical simulation, which uses historical data and assumes that past data represent the full population. Bootstrapping treats the observed sample as a proxy for the population. This distinction is critical:
•  Bootstrapping resamples from the same dataset repeatedly to create a simulated sampling distribution, making no explicit assumptions about the population’s shape.
Simulation of Financial Asset Prices and Returns

•  Historical simulation uses historical datasets directly, relying on the actual sequence of events and treating them as fixed. Bootstrapping is particularly valuable when the true population distribution is unknown but can be reasonably inferred from the available data. In finance, we can never be completely certain of the true population distribution. This approach is effec­ tive when there is a high degree of evidence that the sample is representative of the future distribution, particularly in comparison to parametric approaches that rely on historically derived standard deviations and correlations and that assume normality. Its flexibility and minimal assumptions make it a powerful tool in statistical inference and modeling. Exhibit 12 compares historical simulation and bootstrapping. Exhibit 12: Comparison of Historical Simulation and Bootstrapping Feature Historical Simulation Bootstrapping Source of data Historical dataset Observed sample Sampling method Simple sampling of histori­ cal data Resampling with replace­ ment from the sample Assumptions Assumes past data reflects future Assumes sample represents population Primary use cases Risk management, financial stress tests Estimating confidence inter­ vals, standard errors Computational intensity Low to moderate Moderate By using the observed sample as a proxy for the unknown population, bootstrapping eliminates the need for external data or theoretical models, making it extremely flex­ ible and widely applicable in situations where we have little prior information about the population distribution. Implementing Bootstrapping The value of bootstrapping lies in its ability to avoid making distributional assumptions. It provides a basis for constructing confidence intervals around estimates, assessing the “stability” of an estimate, and offers ease of implementation, among other bene­ fits. Its effectiveness largely depends on how representative the sample is of the true distribution. Larger sample sizes are preferable to smaller ones because they tend to be more accurate representations of the underlying population. Note that regardless of the simulation task, the only functional change in simulation when using the bootstrap method is the source of the scenarios. These models build on the concept of a riskless portfolio that combines a long option position with a short stock position to eliminate sensitivity to price changes in the underlying asset. This approach allows the option to be valued by assuming the stock’s expected return equals the risk-free rate. Features of Bootstrapping Simulations Bootstrap simulation serves as a valuable complement to analytical methods in finan­ cial analysis. While it provides statistical estimates based on empirical distributions derived from historical price data and processes, these results are not exact. Analytical methods, when available, offer deeper insights into cause-and-effect relationships and underlying mechanisms. The bootstrap method’s primary advantage lies in its ability to circumvent explicit distributional assumptions. This feature proves particularly valuable when historical patterns in the data are expected to persist in the future or the underlying distribution is complex or cannot be adequately modeled using standard parametric distributions (e.g., normal, Student’s t). This technique is especially useful in financial applications where price movements and market behavior often deviate from theoretical distributions, exhibiting such characteristics as fat tails, skewness, and time-varying volatility. The strengths of bootstrapping include the following:

Simulation of Financial Asset Prices and Returns • Minimal assumptions: Bootstrapping does not require assumptions about the underlying population distribution—for example, normality. This makes it highly flexible and useful when the true distribution is unknown or difficult to model. • Statistical robustness: Unlike many other methods, bootstrapping is particularly useful when dealing with small datasets. Even with limited data, bootstrapping can help generate a reliable estimate of the variability of a statistic.

•  Simplicity: Conceptually, bootstrapping is straightforward to implement. By resampling with replacement from the observed data, it eliminates the need for complex analytical solutions or parametric models.

•  Robust variability estimates: Bootstrapping provides robust estimates of the variability—standard error—of a statistic and can be used to construct confidence intervals. This makes it an essential tool for hypothesis testing and assessing uncertainty. Bootstrapping also reduces the impact of outliers in the data, relative to historical simulation.

•  Adaptability: Bootstrapping can be applied to almost any statistic (e.g., mean, median, variance, correlation) in various fields, from finance to biol­ ogy, wherever the data structure is complex or non-parametric.

•  No need for a “large” external dataset: Unlike such methods as Monte Carlo and historical simulation, which depend on either theoretical distributions or larger amounts of past historical data, bootstrapping works directly from the sample at hand, making it ideal for situations where data are scarce. The weaknesses of bootstrapping include the following:

•  Computationally intensive: While simple to understand, bootstrapping can be computationally demanding, especially when generating thousands or tens of thousands of resamples. This can lead to long processing times, par­ ticularly with large datasets or when analyzing multiple statistics.

•  Sensitive to sample quality: Bootstrapping assumes that the sample is rep­ resentative of the population. If the sample is biased or unrepresentative, the bootstrap results will be misleading because the method amplifies any existing flaws in the dataset.

•  Not ideal for autocorrelated time-series data: Bootstrapping breaks tempo­ ral dependencies, such as inherent autocorrelation that may be present in financial time series. For such data, specialized methods may be needed to maintain the temporal dependence between observations.

•  Limited extrapolation: Bootstrapping cannot simulate scenarios outside the range of the observed data. In situations where extreme or hypothetical out­ comes are important (such as tail risk events), such methods as Monte Carlo may be more appropriate.

•  No analytical insight: Bootstrapping is purely empirical and does not pro­ vide theoretical insight into the population or the underlying process. It is useful for estimation but does not explain why the data behave in a certain way.
