Glossary G-1 Absolute dispersion The amount of variability or spread in a set of data, without comparing it to any specific reference point or benchmark. Absolute risk aversion A measure of the decline in an inves­ tor’s utility with each incremental increase in risk, holding wealth constant. Actual returns  Returns on an investment after the investment period has ended that may differ from expected returns. Also known as ex post returns or realized returns. After-tax nominal return The total return minus any allow­ ances for capital gains taxes on realized gains and for income taxes on investment distributions. Alternative data Information collected from non-traditional sources, such as social media, satellite imagery, and web traffic, that extends beyond traditional data. Alternative hypothesis  The complement to the null hypothe­ sis, and the null and the alternative hypotheses are mutually exclusive and exhaustive for the values of the parameter being tested. Analytic pricing formula A formula for calculating the price of a financial asset, not always in closed form. Annuity A fixed-income stream of periodic cash flows paid or received over a finite period, without a final lump-sum or bullet repayment. Annuity contracts A financial product that pays out a fixed stream of payments during the life of the contract. A posteriori probability  The probability of an event or hypoth­ esis after incorporating or conditioned on new evidence derived using Bayes’ theorem. Also known as posterior probability. A priori probability The probability of an event or hypothesis before considering new data; reflects pre-existing beliefs based on prior knowledge. Also known as prior probability. Arithmetic–geometric mean inequality For any set of non-negative real numbers, the geometric mean is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean. Arithmetic mean return The simple average of all holding period returns. Also known as arithmetic average return. Artificial intelligence (AI) Technologies enabling computers to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as pattern recognition and decision-making. Asian-style options  Options with payoffs based on the average price of the underlying asset during the option’s life. Autocorrelation  A condition in regression analysis where the residuals are correlated across observations, violating the assumption of independence. Average Quantifies the central tendency and is the sum of all values in a dataset divided by the number of values. Also called mean. Backpropagation An algorithm used to train neural net­ works by adjusting weights in response to errors between predicted and actual outputs, improving model accuracy. Basis point (bp) A unit of measurement that equals 0.01% (1/100th of a percent), or 0.0001 in decimal form. Bayes’ theorem A process of updating the probabilities of hypotheses when given evidence by refining initial beliefs, or a priori probabilities, in light of additional data, or a posteriori probability. Also known as Bayes’ rule or Bayes’ formula. Bernoulli distribution Discrete distribution with one trial and two possible outcomes, where success occurs with probability p and failure occurs with probability 1 − p. Bessel’s correction  An adjustment made to the calculation of sample variance to make these statistics unbiased estima­ tors of the population variance and standard deviation by using (n – 1) instead of the same size, n, in the denominator. Best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) An estimator that is both unbiased and efficient among all estimators that are linear combinations of the data. Beta A measure of the sensitivity of price changes in a par­ ticular asset relative to changes in the market portfolio. This is a measure of systematic risk, risk that cannot be diversified away. Big data Immense volumes of structured and unstructured data characterized by high volume, velocity, variety, and veracity, generated from various sources. Binomial distribution Distribution where one models the outcomes in a fixed number of independent trials, where each trial has two possible outcomes: success or failure. It builds on the Bernoulli distribution. Black–Scholes–Merton formula A closed-form formula to value plain-vanilla European-style calls and puts. Bootstrapping Resamples historical data with replacement to create synthetic datasets, preserving distribution while introducing randomness. Also called bootstrap simulation. Bootstrap simulation  Resamples historical data with replace­ ment to create synthetic datasets, preserving distribution while introducing randomness. Also called bootstrapping. Business risk The risk inherent to the nature of a firm’s operations. Call option Allows an investor to buy the underlying asset at a predetermined price in the future. Capital allocation line (CAL) A depiction of all combinations of risk and return achieved by blending a risk-free asset with a specific risky portfolio. Capital appreciation return The change in price between the time of an initial investment and the price at some later valuation date. Also known as price return. Capital asset pricing model (CAPM) A simple market equi­ librium framework that relates an asset’s expected return to its systematic (market) risk, measured by beta. Capital distribution return Return on distributions received through cash dividends, interest payments, or other types of capital distributions. Capital market line (CML) A special case of the CAL repre­ senting optimal portfolios that mix a risk-free asset with the market portfolio. Cash flow additivity principle The principle that cash flows occurring at the same point in time can simply be added and the present value will not change.

G-2 Glossary Central limit theorem (CLT)  Random samples from any distri­ bution with a finite mean and finite variance will converge to a normal distribution as the sample sizes increase. Cholesky decomposition  A technique for matrix factorization; used to generate correlated random variables. Closed-form solution An exact solution derived through standard mathematical operations without approximations. Cluster sampling A sampling method that divides the popu­ lation into mini-representative clusters, from which entire clusters are randomly selected. Coefficient of determination R squared, R2. A statistical measure representing the proportion of variance in the dependent variable that is explained by the independent variable(s). Coefficient of variation (CV) A standardized measure of dis­ persion, the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean. It is useful for comparing the relative variability of datasets with different units or means. Conditional covariance Measure of the co-movement of two variables, given the condition on a third variable. Conditional mean The expected value of a random variable given that a certain condition is true. Conditional variance The dispersion of a random variable around its conditional mean. Confidence intervals A probabilistic range of values con­ structed from sample data to provide a specified probability of containing the true parameter value. Confidence level  The complement of the levels of significance, α%, representing the probability that the interval contains the true parameter value, (1 – α)%. Consistent estimator An estimator that converges to the true parameter value as the sample size increases. Constituent securities Securities that make up an index. Contingency table Tabular representation that summarizes the relationship between several categorical variables. Contingent claim security A security whose value depends on the price of an underlying asset. Continuously compounded return The natural logarithm of the ratio of the ending total value and starting total value for a given period. Also known as logarithmic return. Continuous random variable A random variable with an infinite number of possible values within a given range. Continuous uniform distribution A probability distribution where all outcomes within a specified range are equally likely. Often, the range is between 0 and 1. Convenience sampling  A sampling method involving selecting accessible elements quickly and at low cost. It may be use­ ful for preliminary studies, but it may also provide biased estimates of population parameters. Copulas Mathematical functions that couple multivariate distribution functions, capturing dependencies between random variables. Corpora A large and structured collection of texts or datasets used to develop, train, and refine algorithms, especially in natural language processing and machine learning. Correlation  Quantifies the degree to which two variables move in a linear relationship with each other. Correlation matrix A table that shows the strength and direc­ tion of linear relationships between asset returns, with val­ ues ranging from −1 to 1 and diagonal elements equal to 1. Coupon bonds  Bonds with intermediate, periodic, cash interest payments, and a final repayment of the principal amount borrowed. Covariance  Quantifies the joint variability of two random vari­ ables. If the variables tend to show similar co-movements, the covariance is positive; if they show opposite behavior, it is negative. Covariance matrix  A table that shows how asset returns move together, with variances on the diagonal and covariances on the off-diagonal. Credit risk  The risk that relates to the possibility that an obligor may not be able to meet its debt obligations. Critical values Values determined by the chosen levels of significance and the test’s probability distribution that depends on the nature of the data and the specific test. Cross-sectional data  This type of data reflects multiple entities at the same point in time, such as different companies in the same year. Cumulative distribution function (CDF)  Gives the probability that the random variable X takes on a value less than or equal to x. Current yield The annual coupon payments divided by the market price of the bond. Data lakes Centralized repositories that store large volumes of structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data in their original format for flexible processing and analysis. Data leakage A situation when information from outside the intended training dataset inadvertently influences the model’s learning process, leading to overly optimistic per­ formance during training but poor generalization. Data mining  A subset of data science that specifically focuses on identifying and extracting patterns, information, and knowledge from very large datasets using series of special­ ized algorithms to uncover hidden patterns. Data science An interdisciplinary field combining statistical methods, mathematical approaches, computational tools, and domain-specific knowledge. Decile A quantile division wherein the interval size is 10% of the data observations. Decision tree Probabilistic analysis of possible future states across distinct paths, each representing a specific outcome with an assigned probability. Also known as probability tree. Deep learning A subset of machine learning where neural networks with multiple hidden layers perform multistage, non-linear data processing to identify complex patterns. Degrees of freedom  The amount of independent information available to estimate parameters of a distribution, with higher degrees indicating more flexibility in the data to estimate these parameters accurately. Dependent variable  The variable being explained or predicted in a model, often denoted as Y. Diffuse prior  An event that has equal probabilities of occurring. Discount  In the case of bonds, “discount” refers to the amount by which a bond is priced below its face (par) value. Discount rate An interest rate that reflects the risk premium associated with the debt and the borrower. Discrete random variable  A random variable with a countable number of distinct values as outcomes. Dispersion The extent to which observations in a distribution are distributed around the average observation. Measures include variance, standard deviation, and range. Distributed computing frameworks Software systems that enable processing and analysis of large-scale datasets across multiple machines to manage complex computational tasks.

G-3 Glossary Distribution function  Provides a complete description of the probability distribution of X, defining how probabilities are assigned to different values or intervals of values that the random variable can take. Diversification benefit The reduction in overall portfolio risk achieved by combining assets that are not perfectly correlated. Dividend payout ratio The ratio of cash dividends paid to earnings for a period. Dividend yield  The annual per-share dividends for a company divided by the share price. Divisor Normalizes the aggregate reference value of an index to a convenient initial value. Dummy variable See indicator variable. Efficient frontier A representation of optimal portfolios that offer the highest return for each risk level or minimize risk for a given return. Also known as Markowitz efficient frontier. Efficient set  A set of portfolios that either maximize return for a given risk or minimize risk for a given return, forming part of the efficient frontier. Embedded options Rights embedded in financial contracts, such as a mortgage borrower's right to early repayment. Epochs Model training cycles in which the entire training dataset undergoes a complete pass through. Specifically used in data science. Equal weighting  Weighs each constituent security in an index equally. Error term In the population regression model, the difference between the observed value and the expected value of the dependent variable given the independent variables, representing unobserved factors affecting the dependent variable. Estimation  The sample mean is a point estimate around which a confidence interval can be constructed to likely include the population mean. European-style call option An option that is only exercisable on a given date. Excess kurtosis The degree of peakedness or flatness in a distribution compared to the normal distribution, which has a kurtosis of 3. Excess returns The difference between an asset’s return and the return on some reference rate, such as the risk-free rate or a market benchmark. Expectation operator  The expected value of a random variable. Expected returns Expected returns on an investment over a specified period, and as such, they are not guaranteed but are estimated based on historical data, current market conditions, and analysis of the asset or investment. Also known as anticipated returns or ex ante returns. Expected value  The average outcome of a random variable over an infinite number of trials. Also known as unconditional expectation or unconditional mean. Fat-tailed distribution A distribution that has heavier tails than a normal distribution, indicating a higher likelihood of extreme values. Also called long-tailed or leptokurtic distribution. Feasible portfolios Combinations of available assets created by adjusting their weights. Financial assets Cash, or a contractual claim on something of value, and includes equity, the ownership claim, debt, claim on specific future cash flows, and hybrids. Financial data science A specialized branch of data science applying its principles specifically to financial data to sup­ port investment, trading, and risk assessment decisions. Financial indicators Observable but not directly tradable indicators and metrics of value, such as exchange rates, interest rates, and market indexes. Financial instruments  Financial assets and other instruments that derive their value from other financial or tangible assets and include derivatives. Financial risk The risk that there can be losses arising from investing and/or the use of financial leverage (or debt) due to fluctuations in prices. Fintech Technological innovations in the design and delivery of financial services and products. Forward price-to-earnings ratio  A price-to-earnings ratio calculated on the basis of a forecast of earnings per share; a stock’s current price divided by next year’s expected earnings per share. Fundamental weighting  Weight of each constituent security within an index based on one or more fundamental factors, such as dividends, earnings, or assets. Gaussian distribution A continuous probability distribution characterized by a symmetrical, bell-shaped curve, and defined completely by its mean and standard deviation. It is a cornerstone of statistical analysis. The “bell” shape means that observations near the mean are more likely than those away from it. Also known as normal distribution. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) Neural networks comprising a generator and a discriminator that work together to produce realistic synthetic data. Generative AI Artificial intelligence systems that create new content, data, or solutions based on patterns extracted from existing data. Geometric average return Represents the average rate at which an asset’s value grows over time, accounting for the compounding of returns. Also known as the geometric mean return. Global minimum-variance portfolio The portfolio of risky assets with the lowest possible standard deviation among all feasible portfolios. Gradient descent An optimization algorithm that iteratively adjusts parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient to minimize a loss function. Gross return  The return earned by a manager after deducting trading expenses, commissions, and similar fees directly associated with generating investment returns. Hedge ratio The optimal proportion of a hedging instrument needed to mitigate the risk in an underlying position. Heteroskedasticity  A condition where the variance of the error terms varies across observations, violating the assumption of homoskedasticity. Hidden layers Intermediate layers in a neural network where data transformations occur, refining features to reveal underlying patterns. High-frequency data Data that are collected or recorded at extremely short intervals, such as milliseconds or microseconds. High-frequency trading (HFT) A type of trading using pow­ erful computers to take advantage of small price changes by algorithmically buying and selling financial assets at extremely fast speeds. Historical simulation  Uses real-world historical data to model future outcomes, assessing risks based on past events.

G-4 Glossary Homoskedasticity  A condition where the variance of the error terms is constant across all observations, an assumption in ordinary least squares regression. Hypothesis testing The process of assessing the probability that a sample statistic reflects a specific population param­ eter and objectively evaluating whether the data support a particular hypothesis. Independent variable The variable used to explain changes in the dependent variable, which is often denoted as X. Multiple regression models have two or more independent variables, and these are often denoted by X 1, X 2, ⋯  , X p. Indicator variable A variable that takes the value 1 when a condition is true and 0 otherwise. Also called a dummy variable. Indifference curve A line of all combinations of goods, out­ comes, or portfolios that provide an investor with the same level of utility or satisfaction. Industry risks Risks that are specific to a particular sector or industry within the broader economy. Also called sector risks. Inflation risk The risk that expected inflation deviates from actual inflation and will lead to a loss of purchasing power. Input layer The initial layer in a neural network that receives raw data, with each neuron representing a feature or variable. Intercept The expected value of the dependent variable when all independent variables are zero; it is where the regression line crosses the y-axis. Interest rate risk The uncertainty of returns due to interest rate fluctuations. Interquartile range (IQR) The difference between the 75th and 25th percentiles; represents the range within which the central 50% of the data falls. Issuer risk Risk that encompasses a firm’s business and finan­ cial risks. Joint distributions  The simultaneous distribution of two ran­ dom variables. Judgmental sampling A sampling method that selects ele­ ments based on expertise. Kurtosis  Quantifies the shape of a distribution’s tails in relation to its peak. Large language models (LLMs)  Advanced AI models capable of processing and generating text based on context from vast datasets. Law of large numbers  The convergence of the empirical mean to the unconditional mean under certain conditions over a large number of random trials. Least squares criterion  The objective of ordinary least squares regression wherein we seek to minimize the sum of the squared residuals between observed values and values predicted by the regression model or the error terms. Leptokurtic distribution A distribution that has heavier tails than a normal distribution, indicating a higher likelihood of extreme values. Also called long-tailed or fat-tailed distribution. Levels of significance  Reflects the evidence required for reject­ ing the null hypothesis and depends on the nature of the hypotheses and the severity of potential errors. Leverage The use of debt in addition to an investor’s own capital. Lexical analysis The examination of word frequency and pat­ tern recognition based on keywords and phrases within a document. Linear regression A method used to model the relationship between one dependent and one or more independent variables by fitting a linear equation to the data. Lin-log model  A model where the dependent variable is linear, but the independent variable is logarithmic. Logistic distribution A continuous probability distribution characterized by a symmetric, S-shaped CDF, used in logistic regression and neural networks, defined by its location and scale parameters. Log-lin model A model where the dependent variable is log­ arithmic, but the independent variable is linear. Log-log model  A model where both the dependent and inde­ pendent variables are logarithmic. Log-normal distribution This type of distribution occurs when the logarithm of the variable is normally distributed. Accordingly, the variable is positively skewed and can take only positive values. A popular distribution for asset prices. Long-only portfolio A portfolio that holds only purchased assets, expecting their value to increase. Long–short strategy  An investment strategy that buys assets expected to rise and sells those expected to fall. Loss gradients The rates of change of a model’s loss function in relation to its parameters; they indicate how adjustments to these parameters influence the error. Machine learning (ML) Techniques designed to enable com­ puters to learn from data and make predictions. Macro risks Broad, economy-wide risks that influence the performance of investments. Also called systematic risk. Marginal density  The probability distribution of a single vari­ able within a multivariate distribution that isolates the single variable’s distribution from other variables in the joint distribution. Margin of error The range within which the true population parameter is expected to fall, with a certain level of confi­ dence, representing the amount of random sampling error. It reflects the confidence interval. Market capitalization The product of the total number of outstanding securities of a company and its current market price per share. Market-capitalization weighting  Weighs each constituent security in an index based on the aggregate market capi­ talization of the constituent securities in the index. Market float The proportion of the constituent security that is available to the investing public. Market risk Risk that represents the possibility that market forces will affect the returns of financial assets, instruments, and indicators in an unexpected manner. Market risk premium  The extra return expected from holding a risky market portfolio over a risk-free asset. Markowitz efficient frontier A representation of optimal portfolios that offer the highest return for each risk level or minimize risk for a given return. Also known as efficient frontier. Matrix A rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. Mean Quantifies the central tendency and is the sum of all values in a dataset divided by the number of values. Also called average. Mean absolute deviation Quantifies variability and is the average of the absolute differences between each value in a set of values and the mean of all the values. Mean square error (MSE) The sum of squares error divided by the degrees of freedom.

G-5 Glossary Mean square regression (MSR)  The sum of squares regression divided by the number of independent variables. Mean–variance utility A utility function that represents an investor’s preferences using only two factors: the expected return (mean) and the risk (variance) of an investment portfolio. Measure of central tendency A single value that quantifies a set of data by identifying the central position within that set of data, typically the mean and sometimes the median or mode. Median  The middle value of a dataset when it is ordered from least to greatest. Median absolute deviation Quantifies variability and is the median of the absolute differences between each value in a set of values and the median of all the values. Mesokurtic distribution  A distribution with a kurtosis similar to that of a normal distribution, with a moderate level of peak and tail thickness. Micro risks  Factors specific to the issuer that determine invest­ ment returns based on the firm’s underlying economic characteristics, such as earning power, market position, financial strength captured by its sales and sales growth, operating margins, and return on assets and equity. Also called unsystematic risks. Minimum-variance frontier The set of portfolios with the lowest possible risk for a given expected return. Minimum-variance portfolio The portfolio with the lowest possible variance among all feasible portfolios. Minimum-variance unbiased estimator (MVUE)  An estima­ tor that is both unbiased and efficient, meaning it has the smallest possible standard deviation among all unbiased estimators. Modal interval The range with the highest frequency in a grouped frequency distribution. Mode The most frequently occurring value or values in a dataset. Moments of a statistical distribution A set of values that provide important information about the shape and char­ acteristics of a distribution, including its central location, dispersion, skewness (third moment), and kurtosis (fourth moment). Money-weighted rate of return  A measure of return that takes into account the size and the timing of the cash flows and is equivalent to the IRR. Also known as dollar-weighted rate of return. Monte Carlo simulation A computational method that uses repeated random sampling to estimate the behavior and outcomes of a complex system or process. Often, a ran­ dom number is drawn from a uniform distribution which is then transformed to a draw from another distribution. Mortgage A loan secured by real estate property that is typ­ ically repaid over time with a series of regular payments. Mortgage-backed securities Financial instruments backed by mortgage loan pools, with payments from mortgage interest and principal. Multiple linear regression A statistical method that models the relationship between a dependent variable and two or more independent variables by fitting a linear equation to the observed data. Mutual fund theorem The theory that the market portfolio is mean–variance efficient and has the highest Sharpe Ratio among all portfolios. This result has significant implications for investment management. Natural language processing (NLP)  A field focused on devel­ oping computer programs to analyze and interpret human language. Net return The return to the investor after deducting the investment manager’s management expenses, custodial fees, taxes, or any other costs related directly to the man­ agement and administration of an investment. Neural networks Computational models inspired by biolog­ ical neural systems, consisting of interconnected nodes (neurons) that process data through layers. No-arbitrage principle  Securities with identical risk and return profiles cannot be priced differently without providing an opportunity for risk-free profit. Noisy data Data containing random errors, irrelevant infor­ mation, or inconsistencies that can obscure underlying patterns. Non-parametric tests Statistical tests that do not assume any statistical distribution for the data and that are often appropriate for categorical data or small sample sizes. Non-probability sampling A sampling method that relies on such factors as judgment or convenience, risking non-representative samples. Non-stationary Used to describe time-varying and unstable statistical properties. Non-systematic risk  (also called unsystematic or idiosyncratic risk) The portion of total risk that is unique to a specific company, industry, or asset and can be reduced or elimi­ nated through diversification. Normal distribution A continuous probability distribution characterized by a symmetrical, bell-shaped curve and defined completely by its mean and standard deviation. It is a cornerstone of statistical analysis. The “bell” shape means that observations near the mean are more likely than those away from it. Also known as Gaussian distribution. Null hypothesis A statement about a population parameter assumed to be true, or equal to a parameter, unless refuted by sample evidence. One-factor risk model A model that explains the expected return of an asset based on its systematic risk, measured by its beta relative to the market, such as the CAPM. One-year forward rate The interest rate agreed on today for a loan that will start in one year and mature in two years. Opportunity cost  The value that investors forego by choosing a particular course of action, such as foregoing or delaying consumption. Optimal portfolio  A portfolio that offers the highest expected return for a given level of risk. Optimal risky portfolio Often called tangency portfolio. A non-risk-free portfolio that maximizes the risk–return trade-off, providing the highest possible return per unit of risk. Option premium The price the investor pays for buying an option. Ordinary least squares (OLS) regression A method of esti­ mating linear relationships between variables by finding variables that minimize the sum of squares error (SSE). Outlier An observation in a dataset that lies an abnormal distance from other values in a random sample from a population and can significantly affect the mean and stan­ dard deviation of the data. Output layer The final layer in a neural network that provides the model’s prediction or output.

G-6 Glossary Overfitting Defect of a model learning training data too pre­ cisely, including noise, resulting in poor performance for new, unseen data. Panel data  This type of data includes multiple observations of the same entities over time, combining both cross-sectional and time-series dimensions. Parametric tests  Statistical tests that assume the data follow a certain distribution, typically a normal distribution or its derived variants, and meet assumptions about randomness, sample size, and variance. Path-dependent option An option whose value depends on the price path of the underlying asset. Percentile A quantile division wherein the interval size is 1% of the data observations. Periodic rebalancing Adjusts the weightings of the securities within the index to align with the original target. Perpetual bonds Bonds with no stated maturity date that are not redeemable. Perpetuity  A perpetual annuity, or a set of never-ending level sequential cash flows, with the first cash flow occurring one period from now. p-hacking The manipulation of data analysis until statistically significant results are achieved. Platykurtic distribution A distribution with thinner tails compared to a normal distribution, suggesting a lower likelihood of extreme values. Also called thin-tailed dis­ tribution or short-tailed distribution. Poisson distribution  Distribution that models the number of events occurring within a fixed interval of time or space where said events happen independently at a known con­ stant rate, λ, per unit of time. Portfolio drift A movement of the allocation in a portfolio away from pre-defined objectives due to performance differentials in the underlying assets and/or actions taken by the portfolio managers. Power of the test The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis, which is the complement of the probability of a Type II error. Premium  In the case of bonds, “premium” refers to the amount by which a bond is priced above its face (par) value. In the case of an option, it is the amount paid for the option contract. Price return index An index that only measures the percent­ age change in price, the capital appreciation return. Also known as price index. Price-to-earnings ratio (P/E)  The ratio of share price to earn­ ings per share. Price-weighted index Weighs each constituent security in an index based on the aggregate sum of the price of the constituent securities in the index. Probability density function (PDF) Describes the likelihood of a continuous random variable lying in a small range around a specific value. Probability mass function (PMF) Function that assigns prob­ abilities for a discrete random variable to be equal to some particular value. Probability sampling A sampling method that ensures every member of the population has an equal chance of selection, leading to a representative sample. Probability tree A probabilistic analysis of possible future states across distinct paths, each representing a specific outcome with an assigned probability. Also known as decision tree. Proxy A substitute instrument used for analysis in place of another with insufficient historical data. Pulling  Random variable generation, or the process of drawing a random number from a probability distribution. p-value The probability of observing results as extreme as observed in the sample, assuming the null hypothesis is true. Qualitative data Non-numerical information, such as market sentiment, management quality, environmental consider­ ations, and geopolitical influences. Quantile Division of observations into intervals of equal size or with an equal amount of data. Quantitative data Numerical information, including prices, returns, interest and currency exchange rates, accounting figures, and economic indicators. Quartile A quantile division wherein the interval size is 25% of the data observations. Quintile A quantile division wherein the interval size is 20% of the data observations. Random variable  A variable that with values that are, at least in part, randomly determined. Range The difference between the highest and lowest values in a dataset; a simple measure of dispersion. Realized returns Returns from buying or selling an invest­ ment or receiving capital distribution income from the investment. Real option  The flexibility in making investment decisions that represents the right but not the obligation to undertake certain business initiatives, such as deferring, abandoning, expanding, or contracting a project. Real returns Inflation-adjusted returns. Real risk-free rate  Inflation-adjusted return obtained by invest­ ing in a risk-free government debt. Reconstitution Updating the index’s composition by adding or removing securities to ensure it accurately reflects the intended target market or sector. Regression coefficients  The estimated parameters in a regres­ sion model that quantify the relationship between an independent variable and the dependent variable, indi­ cating how much the dependent variable changes as the independent variable changes. Reinforcement learning Machine learning approach where algorithms learn through trial and error and by receiving rewards or penalties to optimize decision making. Relative dispersion Quantifies the spread or variability of a set of data relative to a benchmark or mean, often used to compare the variability between different datasets. Relative risk aversion  A measure of how risk aversion changes as an investor’s wealth changes. Replicating portfolio A portfolio with the same value and payoff characteristics as the option being valued. Required rate of return  The minimum rate of return an inves­ tor must earn to accept the investment. Resampling  A technique of repeatedly sampling data to make inferences about population parameters. Resampling with replacement  A method where sampled data points are returned to the pool for possible re-selection. Residual In the sample regression model, the difference between the observed value of the dependent variable and the fitted value from the regression equation for the observation.

G-7 Glossary Return-constrained optimization  A method that determines the lowest possible risk available at the specified return level, identifying asset combinations that lie on the efficient frontier. Optimizing for the lowest portfolio risk, σ p, for a desired level of return. Risk The uncertainty regarding the actual or realized return on an investment. Risk-adjusted return optimization  An approach that identifies asset combinations that create portfolios with the highest risk-adjusted returns on the efficient frontier. Optimizing to maximize the Sharpe ratio, E[r p] − r f _ σ p , where r f represents the risk-free rate. Risk-averse investors Investors who prefer less variable or guaranteed outcomes over gambles with higher expected value. Risk-constrained optimization An approach that identifies asset combinations that create portfolios on the efficient frontier, delivering the highest possible returns at a spec­ ified risk level. Optimizing for the highest expected return, E[r p], for a given level of risk. Risk-free rate  The return on an investment without any default or reinvestment risk; typically represented as the return on short-term government bonds. Risk-neutral investors  Investors who are indifferent between gambles and guaranteed outcomes that have the same expected value. Risk preference A description of investors’ attitudes toward risk and how much uncertainty they will accept for poten­ tial gains. Risk premium The additional returns expected for bearing extra risks that vary according to the financial asset type, investment time horizon, and other specific risk factors. Risk–return trade-off The principle that higher potential returns on an investment are generally associated with higher levels of risk. Risk-seeking investors Investors who prefer gambles with uncertain outcomes over guaranteed ones with the same expected value. Risk tolerance The amount of risk an investor is willing to accept to meet their goals. Risky portfolio A collection of assets that has, in aggregation, an uncertain return. Robust  In the context of statistics, robust means that the results are reliable even given the existence or introduction of outliers to the dataset. Robust estimator An estimator that is not unduly affected by outliers or deviations from assumptions, such as the median. Root of time law The standard deviation of a distribution scales with the square root of time. Sampling distribution of a statistic  The distribution of all pos­ sible values that the test statistic under the null hypothesis can assume when computed from samples of the same size randomly drawn from the same population. Sampling error  The difference between the observed value of a statistic and the true population parameter it estimates due to using subsets of the population. Sector risks Risks that are specific to a particular sector or industry within the broader economy. Also called industry risks. Security market index A portfolio of marketable securities representing a given security market, market segment, or asset class. Security market line (SML) A linear relationship, derived from the capital asset pricing model (CAPM), that shows an asset’s expected return as a function of its systematic (market) risk, measured by beta. Self-supervised learning  A learning approach where models ingest large and diverse datasets without explicit labels to capture a broad understanding. Semi-structured data Data that combine elements of both structured and unstructured formats. Semi-variance Quantifies the variability of values that are below the mean of a dataset and can be a measure of the downside return and risk of an investment. Sharpe ratio A measure of the risk-adjusted return of an investment by comparing its excess return (over a risk-free rate) to its standard deviation, capturing how much return is earned per unit of risk. Short selling The practice of profiting from the decline of a security’s price, typically by borrowing shares to sell and later repurchasing them at a lower price. Simple linear regression A statistical method that models the linear relationship between a dependent variable and a single independent variable by fitting a straight line to the data. Simple random sampling A sampling method that surveys a representative sample to compute the sample mean. Simulation A method to predict theoretical outcomes for a system or calculation. Skewness Quantifies the asymmetry of the probability distri­ bution of a real-valued random variable, where positive skewness indicates a distribution with an asymmetric tail extending toward more positive values or the right tail. Slope coefficient The change in the dependent variable asso­ ciated with a one-unit change in the independent variable. Spearman rank correlation coefficient A nonparametric measure of the strength and direction of a monotonic relationship between two ranked variables. Spread The difference between any two rates. Spurious correlation A correlation between two variables that appears to be causally related but is actually due to either coincidence or the presence of a third, unseen factor. Standard deviation The square root of the variance, this statistic measures the amount of variability or dispersion in a set of data. Standard error of the estimate (SEE or se). Also known as the standard error of the regression or root mean square error; it measures the standard deviation of the residuals. Standard error of the mean The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean. Standard normal distribution A special case of the normal distribution with μ = 0 and σ 2  =  1. Stationary  Used to describe statistical properties that remain consistent over time, making statistical methods more applicable and interpretations more accurate. Statistical inference The process of inferring properties of an underlying probability distribution. Stochastic variable The expression typically used in finance for a random variable. Stratified random sampling A sampling method that divides the population into subpopulations (strata) based on vari­ ous representative filtering criteria. Structured data Data organized in tables, commonly stored in databases, where each field represents the same type of information.

G-8 Glossary Style drift A movement of the allocation in a portfolio away from the initially implemented or pre-defined investment style or strategy. Sum of squares error (SSE) The total of the squared differ­ ences between observed and predicted values, represent­ ing unexplained variation. Also known as the sum of the squared residuals. Sum of squares regression (SSR)  The total variation explained by the model, calculated as the squared differences between predicted values and the mean of the dependent variable. Sum of squares total (SST)  The total variation in the dependent variable about its mean. Sum of the squared residuals The total of the squared differ­ ences between observed and predicted values, representing unexplained variation. Also known as the sum of squares error (SSE). Supervised learning Machine learning in which algorithms learn to model relationships based on labeled training data. Systematic risk Broad, economy-wide risk that influences the performance of investments. This unavoidable, inherent market risk that affects all equity securities is also called macro risk. Tangency portfolio A non-risk-free portfolio that maximizes the risk–return trade-off, providing the highest possible return per unit of risk. Also called optimal risky portfolio. Target semi-deviation Quantifies the dispersion in a dataset by focusing on the deviations of the data points below a specified target or threshold value. Terminal value  The expected value of a share at the end of the investment horizon—in effect, the expected selling price. Test dataset A subset of the data that evaluates how well the model predicts on unseen data. Test statistic A value calculated based on a sample that, when used in conjunction with a decision rule, forms the basis for deciding whether to reject the null hypothesis. Text analytics The use of computer programs to analyze and derive meaning from large, unstructured text or voice-based datasets. Thin-tailed distribution A distribution with thinner tails compared to a normal distribution, suggesting a lower likelihood of extreme values. Also called platykurtic dis­ tribution or short-tailed distribution. Time-series data This type of data includes observations over time for the same entity, such as one company or country, over several years. Time value of money  The tradeoff between cash flows received today versus those received on a future date, allowing the comparison of the current or present value of one or more cash flows to those received at different times in the future. Time-weighted rate of return The compound rate of growth of an investment over a given time period, geometrically linking the returns of subperiods determined by each cash flow event. Total probability rule for expected value The expected val­ ues of different possible outcomes of a random variable, weighted by the likelihood of each outcome. Total return  The sum of capital appreciation return and capital distribution return. Training dataset A dataset that allows an algorithm to iden­ tify relationships between inputs and outputs based on historical patterns. Transformers  Neural network architectures designed to handle long-range dependencies in text, capturing context and meaning effectively. Trimmed mean Quantifies the estimate of central tendency by reducing the influence of outliers. Type I error A false positive result that leads to a rejects rejec­ tion of a true null hypothesis. Type II error A false negative result that fails to reject a false null hypothesis. Unbiased estimate  A statistical estimate whose expected value is equal to the value of the population parameter it aims to estimate, ensuring no systematic error in its calculation. Unbiased estimator An estimator whose expected value is equal to the parameter it estimates. Unconditional covariance The direction of the linear rela­ tionship between two random variables. Unconditional expectation  The average outcome of a random variable over an infinite number of trials. Also known as unconditional mean or expected value. Unconditional mean The average outcome of a random vari­ able over an infinite number of trials. Also known as unconditional expectation or expected value. Unconditional standard deviation The square root of the unconditional variance. Unconditional variance The expected squared spread of a random variable around its mean. Underfitting Defect of a model being too simplistic, failing to capture underlying patterns in the data and leading to poor prediction performance. Uniform distribution Probability distribution where each of the outcomes within a specified range is equally likely. It can be either discrete or continuous. Unrealized returns Gains or losses if the investment were sold at the current market price that either only exist on paper or the investment hasn’t yet paid out earned capital distributions. Also known as paper gains. Unstructured data Disparate, unorganized data that cannot be easily represented in tabular form. Unsupervised learning  Machine learning in which algorithms analyze data without labeled outputs to uncover inherent structures and patterns. Unsystematic risks Factors specific to the issuer that deter­ mine investment returns based on the firm’s underlying economic characteristics, such as earning power, market position, financial strength captured by its sales and sales growth, operating margins, and return on assets and equity. Also called micro risks. Utility function A representation of an investor’s preferences that combines both expected return and risk of a portfolio. Validation dataset A dataset used to fine-tune model param­ eters and validate relationships identified during training. Value at risk (VaR)  Quantifies the downside risk and estimates the potential loss with a certain level of confidence for a financial asset, instrument, or portfolio over a specific time period. Variance  σ2, the average of the squared deviations around the population average. Variance–covariance matrix  A rectangular array of numbers or symbols that shows individual asset variances on the diagonal of the matrix and covariances between asset pairs as off-diagonal elements. Variational autoencoders (VAEs)  Neural networks that com­ press data into a compact form and then attempt to recon­ struct them; useful for identifying underlying patterns. Variety  The diversity of data types and formats collected from multiple sources.

G-9 Glossary Varying levels of risk aversion A non-fixed relationship to risk in which an investor’s risk aversion changes as their wealth changes. Velocity The speed at which data are generated and com­ municated, often requiring real-time or nearly real-time processing. Veracity The credibility and reliability of data sources, crucial for ensuring data quality. Visualization The formatting, display, and communication of data in an understandable graphical form. Volatility  Quantifies the degree of variation over time, typically measured by the standard deviation. Volatility clustering A phenomenon where high- or low-volatility periods follow similar periods. Volume The amount of data included in a dataset. Winsorized mean Quantifies central tendency by replacing the smallest and largest values in a dataset with the values closest to them, thereby reducing the effect of outliers. Yield-to-maturity (YTM)  The internal rate of return of a bond’s cash flows under constant interest rates where the received intermediate cash payments are reinvested at the same rate as the yield-to-maturity. Zero-coupon bonds Bonds that do not pay a coupon but are priced at a discount and pay their full face value at maturity. Z-score  The number of standard deviations the observation is from the mean in a standard normal distribution.
